#5055. Australia passes bill that would let people sue AI chatbot providers

The right to sue would start 12 months after Royal Assent and apply when a covered provider’s safety breach causes loss or damage.

Australia’s Parliament passed the Digital Duty of Care bill on Nov. 25, giving people a future route to sue covered AI chatbot providers over loss or damage caused by a breach of the new online safety duty. Both the duty and the right to sue are due to take effect 12 months after Royal Assent.

The Nov. 25 vote completed the bill’s passage through Parliament. Schedule 2 of Australia’s Digital Duty of Care bill sets out the safety duty and the private right of action. The Senate committee’s report sets out the transition period for that schedule. The communications department confirmed on Nov. 27 that the duty would start 12 months after Royal Assent.

A different part of the bill follows an earlier timetable. Schedule 1, including expanded powers for the eSafety Commissioner over apps and websites used to generate fake nude material, is due to take effect the day after Royal Assent.

Expanded eSafety powers start sooner than the digital duty and the court remedy.

The court remedy follows the 12-month timetable.

Calendar dates depend on when Royal Assent occurs. Branches show the sequence only.

Maps commencement rules for schedules 1 and 2 and the dated passage by Parliament. Connector lengths show sequence and branching.

Calendar dates depend on when Royal Assent occurs. Branches show the sequence only.

Section 28D covers providers of services that use an internet carriage service to generate material with AI. That brings covered AI chatbots within the scope of the private court remedy. The provision also names social media services, relevant electronic services and designated internet services.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

A claimant would need to show that the provider failed to comply with its safety duty and that the failure caused their loss or damage. The bill treats that connection as established if the breach substantially contributed to the loss or damage.

The duty requires providers to take appropriate safety measures, including effective steps to address the risks they identify in their assessments. The explanatory memorandum, quoted by the Senate committee, says a harmful interaction does not necessarily establish a breach. The provider’s response to reasonably foreseeable risks matters, including whether it put effective safeguards in place and kept them working.

If a claim succeeds, the court could award damages, including for emotional distress, issue an injunction or order the provider to apologize. The bill gives courts discretion to choose a remedy suited to the circumstances.

The time limit for bringing a claim is tied to the claimant’s age and the date they suffered the loss or damage. Under section 28E, proceedings must begin before the later of their 21st birthday or six years after the day they suffered the loss or damage.

For someone who is already 21 when they suffer the loss, the six-year period gives the later date. For someone who suffers loss or damage as a child, the 21st birthday can be the later date, depending on their age when they suffered the loss.

Bitcoin's 90-day correlation with gold has reached its highest level on record, according to Galaxy Research data. The measure peaked at 0.56 on Oct. 22 and broke the previous record of 0.50, which Galaxy dated to Nov. 6, 2020.

Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy Digital, posted about the record on X on Friday. "Bitcoin isn't digital gold? Bitcoin reaches highest correlation to gold of all time," he wrote.

Thorn shared two Galaxy Research charts together with the post. According to the charts, the 90-day correlation was at 0.54 on Nov. 23, and the 30-day correlation stood at 0.59 on the same day.

In the first half of 2026, the 90-day correlation stayed near 0.1. It started to rise in July and climbed above 0.50 by early October, according to Galaxy's data. Between 2020 and 2025, the average reading was 0.11.

On Jan. 20, Galaxy CEO Mike Novogratz wrote on X that "the gold price is telling us we are losing reserve currency status at an accelerating rate." "$BTC is disappointing as it is still being met with selling," he added.

Thorn wrote about Bitcoin and gold on X in February. "Bitcoin's failure to trade like gold as part of 'the debasement trade' since Sep. '25 damaged its narrative with new entrants," he wrote. "When bitcoiners said 'digital gold,' they were describing its fundamental properties, not that it's high beta to gold today," he added.

On Wednesday, Galaxy published a report that withdrew its Oct. 26 call on the Bitcoin bear market. "We withdraw our call that the bear market ended in June," the report said. Thorn shared it on X with the comment, "As it turns out, the Bitcoin bear market is definitely not over."

According to the report, Bitcoin closed the week ended Nov. 22 at $61,104 after seven straight weekly losses. Thorn wrote in the report that the level to watch was $58,525, Bitcoin's closing low from June 30. According to Thorn, a daily close below that level would mark "the start of a move to a materially lower low."

"The clock says this bear is overdue to end; the depth says it has further to fall," the report said. On Nov. 22, the bear market was 412 days old, and earlier ones lasted 163 to 406 days from high to low, according to Galaxy.

Bitcoin was down 53% from its October 2025 record at that point. In past bear markets, it lost 77% to 93%. If the June low breaks, Galaxy sees possible new lows at about $48,500 and $28,200.

Galaxy tracks 13 bottom signals, and two of them have been met so far. According to the report, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETPs held about 1.24 million BTC, down 71,339 BTC since Oct. 4.

On Nov. 17, SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci asked Novogratz at the Digital Assets Forum in New York whether Bitcoin could return to $90,000 by the end of 2026. "Unlikely now," Novogratz said. "Less likely than it was. You need something to happen," he added.

#5052. 5 Ways To Prioritize Your Brain Health

From understanding your risk factors to adopting brain-healthy routines, here’s how to take a more proactive role in your cognitive health.

One of the body’s most vital organs—the brain—can be overlooked, even though it guides nearly everything we do.

At its core, brain health is about how well your body’s command center functions—processing emotions, coordinating movement, and interpreting what you see, hear, taste, touch, and smell. It also includes cognitive health—your ability to think, learn, and remember.

Because the brain plays such a central role in everyday life, you don’t have to wait until something feels off to start taking care of it. Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease can begin about 20 years before symptoms appear, making a proactive approach to brain health an important part of caring for your overall health.

This messaging inspired actress, author, and advocate Julianne Moore to partner with Eli Lilly and Company on their Brain Health Matters campaign to encourage people to prioritize their brain health. “From my conversations with people living with Alzheimer’s disease, I’ve seen how much proactive care matters,” Moore says. “That’s why I’m helping to encourage everyone to prioritize their brain health through regular conversations with their doctors.”

Not sure where to begin? Here are five ways to make brain health a priority part in your overall health.

You might not have any concerns about cognitive decline, much less dementia. But taking a proactive approach to cognitive health doesn’t have to wait until later in life—or until something feels off. One brain change associated with Alzheimer’s disease involves amyloid, a protein the body produces naturally. Talking to your doctor can help you understand your personal risk factors and discuss whether steps such as establishing a cognitive baseline and adopting brain-healthy habits may be appropriate for you.

Add brain health to your “must-ask” list for medical appointments and come prepared with specific questions to guide the conversation. Ask your doctor whether a cognitive assessment is appropriate for you. This spoken, written, or digital evaluation can provide a starting point for monitoring your memory and thinking over time.

While a cognitive assessment cannot diagnose a condition on its own, establishing a baseline and completing follow-up assessments as recommended by your doctor may help spot early signs of memory and thinking issues and monitor changes over time.

Here’s what you may want to ask your doctor:

Research shows that up to 45 percent of dementia cases, including those caused by Alzheimer’s disease, may be prevented or delayed by managing changeable risk factors. These include blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes; lifestyle habits around diet, exercise, alcohol consumption, and smoking; and even hearing loss, depression, traumatic brain injury (TBI), and sleep.

You can’t change everything that affects your risk—such as age, family history, or certain genetic markers. But your doctor can help you understand the risk factors that may apply to you and build a plan to manage those that can be changed. The following brain-healthy habits can be a good place to start:

Once you understand your risk factors, establish a cognitive baseline, and identify brain-healthy habits that could work for you, the next step is bringing those pieces together. Work with your doctor to create a plan based on your individual health needs.

Your plan might include ways to manage changeable risk factors, behaviors that support your brain health, and a schedule for revisiting your cognitive health with your doctor. Regular conversations with your doctor about these topics can help you take action early and help support your brain health for the future.

Honest discussions around brain health can help go a long way toward reducing stigma and helping others feel more comfortable seeking information, support, and care. Opening up—even in small ways—can make a difference, whether you’re checking in with loved ones, sharing your own concerns, or simply normalizing the topic in everyday life.

“Brain health is something we don’t talk about often enough,” Moore says. “There’s so much fear around cognitive health and even talking to a doctor about getting an assessment. I think it needs to be normalized.”

To learn more about how you can be proactive for your brain health, visit BrainHealthMatters.com.

#5050. Bitcoin dodged one risk from Japan and now faces a Monday reckoning

The currency move cut the dollar cost of repaying unhedged yen loans. Monday’s two-year Japanese bond auction offers a fresh read on short-term yields.

The yen slipped against the dollar on Friday, cutting the dollar cost of repaying fixed, unhedged yen loans for traders who borrowed the currency to buy Bitcoin. Bitcoin held above 60,000 USDT on Binance during Tokyo trading as two measures of the city's November inflation moved in opposite directions. Monday's two-year government bond auction is the next chance to see whether the yen and short-term yields move higher together.

The Statistics Bureau of Japan said preliminary consumer prices across Tokyo's 23 wards rose 2.9% from a year earlier excluding fresh food, up from 2.6% in October. When energy is also excluded, inflation slowed to 2.5% from 2.6%. The preliminary Tokyo figures offer an early read ahead of the national release.

Electricity and city gas explain much of the split. Electricity prices rose 9.5% from a year earlier, up from 1.7% in October, and city gas prices rose 13.7%, up from 4.9%. Energy's contribution to the headline inflation rate increased by 0.34 percentage points. The overall rate rose more modestly, to 2.8% from 2.7%, as other categories offset part of that increase. The bureau put the increase in electricity's contribution at 0.22 percentage points, and city gas at 0.11.

Both Tokyo gauges were at 2.6% in October. In November the measure that includes energy rose, while the measure that excludes it slowed.

Electricity and city gas accounted for most of the increase in energy’s contribution to Tokyo’s headline inflation rate.

November values are preliminary and cover Tokyo’s 23 wards. Electricity and city gas are included in the energy total, and the printed contributions are rounded.

The slopes share one vertical scale and use reported year-over-year Tokyo CPI rates. The zero-based bars show the bureau’s reported October-to-November changes in contributions to the all-items rate.

November values are preliminary and cover Tokyo’s 23 wards. Electricity and city gas are included in the energy total, and the printed contributions are rounded.

The dollar bought 159.28 to 159.30 yen at 9 a.m. Friday and 159.33 to 159.35 yen at 5 p.m., according to the Bank of Japan's Friday quotes. That compared with 159.16 to 159.18 yen at 5 p.m. Thursday. Both quotes use Tokyo time.

CoinGlass’s daily Binance data showed Bitcoin trading as low as 60,472 USDT on Nov. 27 as of 11:54 a.m. UTC. CryptoSlate's Bitcoin price tracker put it at $61,529 as of 11:57 a.m. UTC on Friday.

Ahead of the release, the risk for yen-funded Bitcoin trades was that hotter inflation could push the currency and short-term yields higher. An investor who borrows yen to buy Bitcoin and leaves the currency risk unhedged has to buy yen back to repay the loan. When the yen strengthens, the investor needs more dollars to repay the same yen balance even if Bitcoin's dollar price stands still. Friday's weaker yen moved that cost in the other direction.

Interest costs move on a different timetable. A trader pays more in interest if a yen loan has to be replaced at a higher rate. The actual rate and the timing depend on the instrument, maturity and any hedge, so traders with similar Bitcoin positions can face different costs.

Japan's Ministry of Finance has scheduled the November 30 two-year bond auction notice for 10:30 a.m. Tokyo time and the public result for 12:35 p.m. At October’s two-year auction, the yield at the weighted-average accepted price was 1.91%, giving traders a benchmark for the new issue.

The auction yield measures the return implied by the price paid for the new bonds. The two-year yield in secondary trading just before and after the result can show whether investors are repricing the path of Japanese rates. If that market yield rises while the yen strengthens against the dollar, borrowers who need to refinance could face dearer loans just as their outstanding yen debt becomes more expensive in dollars. If yields rise and the yen stays weak, the signals would still be split.

Even a move in both markets would leave open how many Bitcoin positions use yen funding. Bank for International Settlements researchers documented how hard it was to size the broader currency carry trade after the August 2024 unwind.

#5049. Bitcoin Developer Warns Google Play Policy Could Lead to Home Invasions

On Nov. 27, Bitcoin developer Peter Todd warned that Google's plan to publicly display developers' addresses on the Play Store could lead to home invasions targeting developers of Bitcoin apps.

For independent developers working from home, the address displayed on Google Play could also be their residential address.

"There will be home invasions to compromise developers," Todd wrote on X.

He specifically highlighted the risks to developers of Bitcoin and other security-related apps, urging Google employees responsible for implementing the change to refuse to do so.

Starting March 1, 2027, Google Play will display the phone number and address of developers who use individual accounts to publish apps and identify themselves as traders.

Google explained that the requirement is related to its obligations as an online marketplace in the European Economic Area (EEA) and the UK.

The address and contact information will be visible to Play Store users worldwide.

The question is what address a developer might have to disclose, even for a relatively small app.

Dodemaide explained that Google support had informed him that he couldn't use a post office box because the address had to match his verified residential address.

He said he was considering removing his app from 31 countries to protect his home address.

Dodemaide also asked whether Google would allow individual developers to use a verified business mailing address instead.

Google lists several types of developers who may need to consider whether they qualify as traders, including those who sell apps, offer in-app purchases or earn advertising revenue.

For example, someone publishing an app purely as a hobby could declare themselves a non-trader.

Developers who don't distribute their apps in the EEA or UK are also considered non-traders under the policy.

Existing account holders have until Feb. 1, 2027, to submit their trader declarations, one month before the contact information becomes publicly visible.

Developers creating new accounts will need to make their declarations during account registration.

Google warns that failing to comply could prevent developers from updating their apps or result in their apps being removed from the Play Store globally.

#5047. Trying to Build Muscle and Lose Fat? Don’t Overlook This Part of Body Recomp

Crushing your workouts is only half the equation.

When it comes to body recomposition, showing up and crushing your workouts is only half the equation. You also need to pay attention to your nutrition to build muscle and lose fat.

And that part of the job isn’t always as straightforward as exercise. In the gym, you know you need to regularly lift enough to challenge your muscles and get your cardio in. In the kitchen, body recomposition typically involves two key things: getting enough protein and managing your calorie intake. As simple as that sounds, it isn’t always easy.

There are a few ways to approach these goals, but one key to making them more sustainable and manageable (and therefore easier to stick to!) is to track your macronutrients, or macros. The three macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats, and protein, and each plays a unique role in your body recomposition journey.

Carbs get a lot of unnecessary hate, but they’re your body’s primary energy source, says Dana White, RD. Your body relies on glucose, a sugar that is broken down from carbs. Without enough of it, your energy, concentration, and mood can all be affected.

Fats are vital to your body’s overall functioning. They support the health of your cells, help your body absorb vitamins like A, D, E, and K, and play a big role in satiety, White says. Protein, perhaps the most obvious of the three, plays a major role in muscle repair and development—important at any time, but especially on a body recomp journey.

Counting your macros can help you stay on track with your body recomposition journey. To find out how much of each macro you need and how to fill your plate, try our Eating for Body Recomp Guide.

The XRP Ledger's native lending protocol entered a 14-day activation countdown on Friday after its amendments gained 29 of 35 validator votes, according to XRPScan. If support holds, the ledger will get native lending and borrowing as early as Dec. 11, for the first time since its launch in 2012.

Hussein Zangana, director of community at the XRP Ledger Foundation, cast the 29th vote with his validator and announced it in an X post on Friday. "I vote now for the Lending Protocol on the XRP Ledger and it's now in activation with 29 Yes votes," Zangana wrote.

𝗜 𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 Lending Protocol 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 XRP Ledger and it's now in activation with 29 Yes votes. 𝗩𝗲𝘁 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀📝: Lending and borrowing unlock capital and liquidity on the XRP Ledger, provide yield and make XRP and XRPL assets usable as collateral. I appreciate the efforts exercised by the community to give this amendment a good screening! For validators this is important assistance and help in making educated decisions. Let's dive into why i voted Yes for Lending on XRP🧵.

According to XRPScan, LendingProtocol and its update LendingProtocolV1_1 both reached 29 votes on Friday. The earliest activation date for LendingProtocolV1_1 is Dec. 11, and its support has to stay above 80% until then. SingleAssetVault, the third amendment in the package, has 30 votes and can activate as early as Dec. 9.

"Lending and borrowing unlock capital and liquidity on the XRP Ledger, provide yield and make XRP and XRPL assets usable as collateral," Zangana added in the same post.

Ripple engineer Vito Tumas first proposed the protocol in April 2024. According to the XLS-65 standard, each Single Asset Vault holds only one asset, such as XRP or RLUSD, and depositors get vault shares in the form of Multi-Purpose Tokens.

Under XLS-66, a loan broker uses that capital to issue loans with a fixed term and a fixed rate. The broker checks borrowers off-chain and can post its own first-loss capital to cover defaults. Interest payments go back into the vault, and the protocol has no on-chain liquidations.

"Represent value. Move value. Trade value. Now: finance value," Jazzi Cooper, head of product at RippleX, wrote on X about the vote. According to Cooper, the team made "deliberate design decisions: protocol native, built-in compliance, and off-chain underwriting."

J. Ayo Akinyele, head of engineering at RippleX, wrote that the vaults and the protocol went through "multiple independent audits, a public Attackathon, formal verification, AI-assisted reviews, community testing, and validator review." Ripple and Common Prefix did the formal verification in the Lean 4 theorem prover. "Traditional testing isn't enough when you're building DeFi directly into Layer-1," Tumas wrote.

Clearpool said that it would bring "real-world, institutional-ready lending infrastructure, built natively on XRPL." The platform plans a credit fund on the ledger with Ripple and Cicada Partners, and it has already tested a full loan cycle on Devnet. "We want to make real loans to real businesses," Tom Lombardi of Cicada Partners said.

Evernorth CEO Ashish Birla said that his company "is exploring how XLS-66 could support yield generation as part of our broader treasury strategy."

According to XRPScan, SingleAssetVault can go live on Dec. 9, and the two lending amendments can follow on Dec. 11 if their support holds.

#5044. Google’s lightweight Gemini matched two top models on a chemistry test

All three identified known compounds in about 97% of attempts when given the same chemistry tools and web access.

Google DeepMind released tools for interpreting mass spectrometry data in its Antigravity AI platform on Nov. 25. In the company’s test, the software helped its lightweight Gemini 3.8 Flash match two frontier models at identifying known compounds. With the tools and internet access, all three identified the exact molecule in about 97% of attempts on a set of 100 compounds whose fragment patterns were already recorded in public libraries.

The models were farther apart with internet access alone. In DeepMind’s benchmark, Flash missed more than three quarters of its attempts to identify a compound, while Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon missed roughly a quarter to a third. All three scored below 4% with neither internet access nor the specialist tools.

DeepMind drew the test spectra from the Enamine REAL collection in the public MoNA library. The compounds’ structures were also cataloged in PubChem. The team screened out recordings in which the molecule had produced too few useful fragments. The benchmark ran three attempts per spectrum. Runs that took more than an hour counted as failures, while temporary infrastructure and quota errors were excluded.

Tandem mass spectrometry measures the charged fragments a molecule breaks into. To identify the molecule, a chemist can compare that pattern with a reference spectrum recorded from a known compound.

For the internet-only runs, DeepMind said scripts written on the fly struggled with noisy peaks and with choosing which masses to search. The new Mass Spec Skills give Antigravity established software to clean up a signal, look for matching reference spectra and check whether a proposed structure fits the measured fragments.

DeepMind also reported that adding the skills reduced the number of tokens each model generated per attempt, with the largest proportional drop for Flash. Flash with the tools was more accurate than either frontier model with internet access alone.

In a test without a spectral-library search, Antigravity used fragment measurements to infer a formula and narrow down candidate structures in PubChem. The compound it selected was already cataloged.

For a compound that is genuinely new, a predicted formula and explanations for some of the peaks can give a chemist a starting point. DeepMind says some structures, including mirror-image molecules, break apart in such similar ways that telling them apart can take another kind of lab measurement.

#5042. ‘Give It Up’: Saylor Fires Back at Infamous Bitcoin Critic

When American entrepreneur Jeffrey Tucker told Bitcoiners to stop dreaming about Bitcoin becoming the world's most valuable asset, Strategy co-founder Michael Saylor responded with the example of a gold-backed banknote.

"Give it up, Bitcoiners. There is no such thing as money that is not used in exchange," Tucker wrote on X.

Tucker argued that Bitcoiners had brought the criticism upon themselves. They made the mistake of thinking they could simply declare Bitcoin a store of value and that would somehow make it one. That is not how it works, according to Tucker. He argued that nothing in the history of money supports this idea.

In his response, Saylor started with an example involving a bakery. Suppose someone buys bread at a bakery. They pay for the bread with a gold-backed banknote. The baker can use that banknote to pay the miller.  The miller can use it to pay the farmer. All three transactions could be completed using the same banknote, while the gold stays in the vault.

@jeffreytucker Jeffrey, a gold-backed banknote could pay the baker, the miller, and the farmer while the gold stayed in the vault. Today people pay in dollars and save in gold, stocks, and real estate. Bitcoin is competing for those savings.

In the second part of his response, Saylor made an argument familiar to anyone who gets paid in dollars.

Sure, you can use dollars to buy groceries. However, you can still decide to keep some of your wealth in stocks, gold, or real estate.

"Today people pay in dollars and save in gold, stocks, and real estate. Bitcoin is competing for those savings," Saylor wrote.

This last point was less ambitious than the claim Tucker was pushing back against.

Tucker was talking about Bitcoin becoming the world's most valuable asset.

Saylor, meanwhile, was making a simpler argument about where people choose to keep their savings.

However, Saylor's gold analogy raises an interesting question for Tucker. In Saylor's example, gold is still relevant to the purchase of bread because it backs the banknote the baker accepts.

However, in his modern examples, someone who chooses to save in stocks isn't necessarily concerned about whether their local bakery accepts stocks as payment.

For Tucker, it's all about how the customer pays for a loaf of bread. For Saylor, it's about what the baker does with the money after selling it.

#5041. Should We All Be Seeing a Concierge Doctor?

Paying an out-of-pocket fee could deliver faster, more accessible medical care. What’s the catch?

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

For as long as I can remember, going to my primary care doctor has been simple: I’d schedule an appointment a few weeks (or months) in advance, commute across town for an in-person appointment, and hope that my insurance covered whatever labs were ordered. But lately, many people have been opting for a membership-based system where they pay a monthly or annual fee for on-demand care. This concept is called concierge medicine.

Over the past few years, the number of concierge medicine services like Tia and One Medical has skyrocketed. Between 2018 and 2023, the number of direct primary care and concierge practice sites grew by roughly 83 percent, per a 2025 study in Health Affairs. (But there are also concierge practices specific to gynecology, longevity medicine, and even emergency medicine.)

“Over the course of my career, I've seen a lot of frustrations that patients have had in terms of access to care, long wait times, lack of continuity of care,” says Jane Zhu, MD, a primary care provider and associate professor of medicine at Oregon Health and Science University, and author of the Health Affairs study. There’s a real need for faster, more on-demand medical care—and concierge medicine is one way that patients are getting that.

Membership prices vary, with some costing as little as $9 a month for on-demand urgent and primary care, and others costing as much as $45,000 a year for top-tier care (at-home doctor visits for urgent care, X-ray imaging from your bed, and even private jets on standby for medical evacuation while you’re traveling). If you don’t live in a major city, many of these programs offer telehealth services all over the country.

So, what’s the catch? Ahead, read up on everything you need to know about concierge medicine, including the pros and cons, and who it’s right for.

The premise is simple: paying a membership fee unlocks extra attention and access to care from your doctor.

At most traditional clinics and hospitals, the goal is for doctors to see as many patients a day as possible. (More visits equals more insurance claims and/or copays, which in turn makes money for the practice.) With concierge medicine, doctors don’t operate within this same construct. Instead, they make money from membership fees, which means they can still turn a profit with a much smaller pool of patients. When you schedule an appointment with a concierge doctor, you’re not competing with hundreds of other patients for a time slot in the same way you would for a traditional doctor.

When Kristen Harvey, MD, MPH, a concierge family medicine physician at Mount Sinai, worked in traditional medicine, she only got about 15 to 20 minutes for each patient visit. Now, she has the freedom to extend her visits to 45 to 60 minutes and form closer relationships with her patients. “I'm able to go into deeper discussions from a more holistic perspective and have a different type of conversation,” she says. Talking more in depth about sleep, nutrition, and lifestyle habits in general is key to helping her patients prevent illnesses in the first place—not just treat them when they come up.

Additionally, getting lab work done through concierge medicine may be a smoother process. While some traditional practices may have you drop by LabCorp to get your blood drawn, for example, many concierge practices will just do it on site, and even go beyond your average complete blood count for in-depth lipid, hormone, and genetic panels. But everything isn't always included in the membership, so check before they draw.

When you need a specialist outside of your concierge practice, they’ll often have health navigators—people whose job it is to schedule your appointments for you, facilitate communication between your providers, coordinate prescriptions, and run point on any insurance claims. Because the health care system can feel so fragmented and hard to understand, the health navigation piece is a major highlight for many patients, says Scott Braunstein, MD, an internal and emergency medicine physician and the chief medical officer at Sollis Health, a concierge clinic for urgent and emergency care.

Regarding costs outside of the membership fee and bloodwork, every concierge practice is different. At Tia, for example, preventative care services like yearly physicals or vaccinations are usually covered by insurance, but diagnostic appointments often come with additional out-of-pocket fees. That means that if you come in for a UTI, sick visit, or complaint about a new health problem, it’ll often result in an additional charge on the patient’s end. The average copay for these kinds of visits at Tia is between $15 and $75—not too different from a traditional doctor’s appointment. However, at a high-end program where you pay entirely out of pocket, the care is pretty all-inclusive.

As of now, there isn’t enough data on concierge medicine to determine whether this model provides superior health outcomes for patients—like fewer hospitalizations or better chronic disease management—compared to traditional systems. That being said, there is one undeniable factor that contributes to good health: regularly going to the doctor. A 2026 report by the health policy initiative Milbank Memorial Fund found that people with chronic illnesses who regularly see a primary care provider have lower rates of hospitalization and emergency room visits—and lower health care costs on the whole.

However, in the U.S., about one-third of adults don’t have a usual source of primary care, per the report. Concierge medicine is one way to bridge this gap of primary care access, and give people an easy, on-demand way to take care of their health. Appointments are easier to schedule, can often be taken from your phone or computer, and the experience is designed to just be more enjoyable and convenient. “When we remove barriers for people accessing care, people are more likely to engage in their health. And when people are more likely to engage in their health, they have better health outcomes,” says Natasha Bhuyan, MD, is a primary care provider and the vice president of In-Office Care at One Medical.

If you can get into these models of care, they seem to be beneficial for both the clinician and the patient. But the question remains: “What happens if you can't get into those models of care?” says Dr. Zhu.

The number of clinicians practicing in membership-based clinics grew by 78 percent between 2018 and 2023, per the Health Affairs study. That means that more clinicians are leaving traditional medicine for this model—which could put pressure on an already-stretched-thin primary care system. If more clinicians leave the traditional system, it could become harder for the people who can’t pay for concierge medicine to access the traditional care they need. So while concierge medicine may help some people live healthier lives, it doesn’t yet fix the broader need for more primary care access in the United States, says Dr. Zhu.

The study also found that while concierge medicine providers are growing, the share of physicians actually declined, and the number of advanced practice providers—like nurses, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants—increased. These advanced practice providers were more likely to be new entrants to the workforce with no prior employer. So while there are still concierge providers with a career’s worth of experience, you might be more likely to get a newer provider with less experience if you opt for concierge medicine.

If you’re frustrated with a fragmented health system where you have to be the one to connect the dots between all of your doctors, concierge medicine could be a welcome reprieve. For instance, Dr. Harvey expects to see more and more patients with chronic illnesses opting for concierge models in the next couple of years. If you have a condition like PMOS, for example, you might be seeing five different specialists to deal with the symptoms: a dermatologist, endocrinologist, gynecologist, nutritionist, and a primary care provider.

With a concierge practice that specializes in convenient, wraparound care, you may be able to see multiple of these specialists all in one place, and have a health navigator or coach to help you coordinate appointments, says Dr. Bhuyan. When you’re dealing with complex medical conditions, or just finding yourself going to the doctor a lot for illnesses or infections, paying for extra time and access to your doctor might just make for a better experience.

The term “concierge” can make this form of care seem cost-prohibitive—and some services certainly are. That said, there are a few options with low membership fees that take insurance, including One Medical (starting at $9/month), Sesame Plus ($10.99/month), Tia Signature ($25-a-month membership, only available in some states) and Folx ($44/month).

If you’re using insurance, you’ll have to do your research to determine how much you’ll pay out of pocket. Popular services like Tia, Allara, Folx, and One Medical accept a wide variety of insurance plans, but specify that copays and other fees can vary plan by plan, just like at the regular doctor. If you’re not using insurance, these practices usually specify self-pay costs in addition to the membership fee depending on the visit or service type, and depending on the care you’re looking for, it could be a bargain.

Before committing to a membership anywhere, find out which services will and won’t be covered (like lab testing or imaging), and how easy it is to cancel said membership if you decide it’s not a fit, says Dr. Bhuyan.

A lot of times, you can also find local doctors practicing concierge-style medicine, and there are search tools like MDVIP or NextMD, which connect patients with a network of in-person concierge physicians all over the country. And if you can’t find one near you, there are plenty of large-scale telehealth services at your fingertips. Be sure to research the doctor beforehand to make sure that they’re legit, and that their expertise aligns with your goals, says Dr. Bhuyan.

Overall, health care is shifting more towards patients’ autonomy. They want to “decide how their health care dollars are spent, whether that's through HSA plans or other means. They’re more empowered to choose the service that works for them,” says Dr. Braunstein. So, only you can decide if a concierge doctor is right for you (and your wallet!).

Meet the experts: Jane Zhu, MD, is a primary care provider and Associate Professor of Medicine at Oregon Health and Science University. Kristen Harvey, MD, MPH, is a concierge family medicine physician at Mount Sinai. Scott Braunstein, MD, is an internal and emergency medicine physician and the chief medical officer at Sollis Health, a concierge clinic for urgent and emergency care. Natasha Bhuyan, MD, is a primary care provider and the Vice President of In-Office Care at One Medical, a membership-based in-person and telehealth clinic owned by Amazon.

#5039. How Coldcard’s $112 million Bitcoin exploit slipped past 15 security reviews

Independent researchers repeatedly examined Coldcard's firmware without discovering the vulnerability that ultimately enabled widespread Bitcoin theft.

A security flaw in Coldcard's Bitcoin hardware wallets went undetected for more than five years despite at least 15 independent security research and review efforts.

Coinkite, the wallet's manufacturer, published its postmortem on Nov. 24, detailing how a firmware defect introduced in March 2021 weakened the recovery phrases generated by its devices, enabling attackers to steal customers' Bitcoin without accessing their hardware wallets.

An Aug. 14 analysis by Galaxy Research identified with high confidence 1,778.84 BTC, worth $112.7 million at the time, stolen from more than 8,600 addresses. Galaxy estimated that losses could reach 2,417 BTC, or $153 million, if additional suspected thefts were confirmed.

Coinkite said it had matched approximately 300 loss-related support tickets to 236 customer accounts, representing about 0.2% of its estimated user base. However, the company acknowledged that the actual number of affected customers was likely higher.

The vulnerability originated from a firmware configuration error that caused Coldcard devices to generate recovery phrases using a weaker software-based random number generator instead of the intended hardware component.

The devices continued producing apparently valid recovery phrases, allowing the defect to escape routine security and functionality tests.

Coinkite's postmortem estimates that the defect substantially reduced the randomness protecting recovery phrases across five Coldcard models, including the Mk2, Mk3, Mk4, Mk5 and Q.

Attackers exploited that weakness to reconstruct private keys offline and transfer Bitcoin from affected wallets.

Between 2021 and 2026, Coldcard underwent at least 15 independent security research and review efforts, including two paid third-party product reviews. Its publicly available firmware repository also had 54 contributors.

One commissioned review in March 2022 specifically examined random-number generation and related security measures without discovering the defect.

More recently, independent security researcher Rob Hamilton used OpenAI's Cybersecurity Harness to examine Coldcard's firmware between May 1 and June 26.

The AI-assisted review generated 85 potential security findings, several of which prompted fixes, but failed to identify the seed-generation vulnerability.

A separate June 17 review by security researcher Nick Farrow also examined weak random-number generation and concluded that the relevant implementation was sound.

Coinkite attributed these failures to a gap in its verification process. Existing checks established that the hardware random-number generator was present in the firmware but failed to confirm whether the software actually used it to create recovery phrases.

The company identified the defect on July 30, following the first reported thefts, and released corrected firmware the following day.

Security firm Keylabs subsequently verified the fix across four firmware releases for Coldcard's Mk5 and Q wallets.

Coinkite has also introduced additional safeguards that combine user-provided randomness with multiple hardware sources when generating new recovery phrases.

However, these changes cannot strengthen recovery phrases created using the defective firmware, leaving previously affected wallets exposed even after their owners install the latest updates.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Keylabs traced the seed-generation fix to four signed releases. Owners keeping a wallet still need to know how its original recovery phrase was created.

Coinkite advises moving funds to a fresh wallet if the original seed was affected or its origin is unclear.

The audit covers the seed-generation fix on the four listed standard releases. Coinkite’s migration guide details the qualifying dice exception and secure external imports.

The upper path follows the scope in Keylabs’ October 15 report. The lower path follows Coinkite’s affected-seed migration guidance.

The audit covers the seed-generation fix on the four listed standard releases. Coinkite’s migration guide details the qualifying dice exception and secure external imports.

Coinkite said wallets using securely generated external recovery phrases were unaffected. Owners who incorporated at least 50 fair, independent and private dice rolls during their original wallet setup also remained protected if they followed the prescribed procedure.

The company advises other affected users to generate new recovery phrases using verified firmware and transfer their Bitcoin to the resulting wallets.

Meanwhile, law enforcement continues investigating the thefts, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has opened a separate case.

Coinkite has appealed to whoever controls the stolen Bitcoin to return the funds. Nearly four months after the exploit, however, the company has yet to decide whether it will compensate affected customers.

#5037. Experts Say Weightlifting Is the Fountain of Youth. Here's How to Get Started at Any Age

If you want to age independently—haul your own groceries, get up stairs, and play with your grandkids)—here’s the science-backed secret: lift weights. Yep, those dumbbells in the gym aren’t just for young buffs (you know this!)—and they’re your ticket to keep doing the things you love most.

Getting older doesn’t have to mean getting weaker. In fact, senior weight lifting—doing resistance training with machines and/or free weights in your 60s and beyond—offers physical and mental benefits that make it a vital part of aging well.

Women start losing muscle after 30, and this speeds up after menopause due to dramatic changes in your hormone levels. This change impacts both muscle and bone health, but strength training can help maintain bone density, promote preservation (and even addition!) of muscle, and set your body up for an active, independent life, according to the International Osteoporosis Foundation.

Here, we share all the fundamentals you need to understand why weight lifting and strength training are so important as you age, and how you can (safely!) get started.

Aging gracefully isn't just about staying active; it’s about choosing the right kind of activity to support your health. Resistance training (with bodyweight, free weight, and resistance band exercises) is one of the best ways to counter the effects of aging, helping you build up muscle to support daily activities and prevent conditions like osteopenia and osteoporosis that can lead to bone fractures. And even if you've never lifted a weight before, it's never too late to start.

“Weight training is the fountain of youth,” says Abby Bales, PT, DPT, CSCS, founder of Reform Physical Therapy. “Not only does it help increase and maintain bone density to prevent fractures, but the muscle mass that weight training builds also helps to regulate our blood sugar and metabolism.” Weight lifting can even improve balance and coordination, decreasing the frequency, severity, and likelihood of falls.

Want to gain serious strength? Try our Strong After 50 4-Week workout plan.

On top of the physical benefits, resistance training has shown promise in staving off neurological conditions like Alzheimer’s and dementia, according to a 2023 study published in Frontiers in Neuroscience, making it a multi-benefit tool for aging well. You can think of lifting weights as your body’s best tool to promote resilience, energy, and independence through the aging process.

Starting with small, manageable steps—such as incorporating resistance bands or light weights into your routine—can help you gain confidence and momentum while reaping the long-term benefits.

The best exercises for women over 60 are weight-bearing and promote strength, posture, and/or balance (sometimes all at once!). While the best exercises for each individual depend on factors including medical history, fitness level, and personal preference (a personal trainer or physical therapist can help you design a more personalized plan!), it’s always great to start with fundamental exercises that incorporate movements used in daily life.

To help get you started, here are a few exercises that Bales recommends older women incorporate in their weekly routine.

Instructions: Select five to seven of the exercises below, mixing two to three upper body exercises, two to three lower body, and one or two core. Start with two to three sets of 10 reps of each. If you’re new to strength training, begin by doing the routine once a week and gradually work up to three times per week. Choose a weight that feels heavy enough to make the last two to three reps of each set feel tough, yet achievable.

Time: 15 to 20 minutes | Equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebells, stair or step-up platform | Good for: Full-body

Why it rocks: The air squat mimics many daily activities, such as getting up and down from a toilet seat, standing up from a chair, and bending down to pick something up. All of these activities are important as we age, so make sure you’re doing some form of squatting as you get older to help stay independent and capable of all these tasks and more. This move is also great because it can be done using your body weight alone, although adding a weight to up the intensity is always encouraged.

Pro tip: If getting down low enough or balancing feels too challenging, try doing this with a chair or couch behind you. At the bottom of the move, tap your bum to the seat or briefly pause there before standing back up.

Why it rocks: This exercise helps with strength and mobility in the shoulder joint, which will allow you to reach items in upper cabinets or even put on/take off a T-shirt for years to come.

Why it rocks: As we age, simple things like stepping up onto a curb, walking on uneven surfaces and going up and down stairs can become challenging and increase the risk of tripping or falling. For this reason, it’s important to practice fully picking up the feet and clearing them from the floor. This exercise focuses on just that.

Pro tip: If this is challenging, start by doing it somewhere that you can hold onto a railing or fixed surface with one hand for support. You can also start with a low step or platform—something that’s six inches high or less—and eventually increase the height as the move becomes easier.

Why it rocks: Your biceps help you bend your arm and make it possible to perform daily tasks such as doing your laundry, lifting a heavy pot or pan, and more. Biceps curls are a great way to keep this muscle strong.

Why it rocks: Good posture is important for preventing things like stress fractures, which can occur in women with low bone density due to osteoporosis. This move targets the shoulders, upper back, and biceps all at once, helping to improve posture and strength.

Pro tip: If you’re struggling to hinge forward, try doing it one arm at a time, and use the other arm to hold onto a chair or railing to support you. The more you hinge, the more you will target your back.

Why it rocks: Reverse lunges build strength in the glutes, hamstrings, and quads, while also improving balance and stability to help prevent falls as we age.

Pro tip: This can be a challenging exercise for many people because of the balance aspect, so try holding onto a stable object or countertop with one hand at first.

Why it rocks: Incline pushups are a gentler version of regular pushups, perfect for building arm, shoulder, and chest strength without straining your wrists or shoulders.

Pro tip: Begin with a higher surface to reduce intensity and pressure on the wrists. You can even use a wall! As you improve with this move, gradually lower the incline to make your body more parallel to the floor, which will make the exercise feel more challenging.

Why it rocks: This move is truly a full-body functional exercise that is great for improving balance, strength, and mobility to help older adults get up and down from the floor.

Pro tip: This is a complex move, so it’s best to break it down into smaller parts first. Try it first without weights and start by practicing just one or two pieces of the movement before putting it all together.

Why it rocks: Your triceps are important for extending your elbow, making daily movements possible like pushing yourself up from the ground or supporting your bodyweight with your arms (like in a plank).

Why it rocks: This squat variation has all the perks of a classic squat, but widens the stance to target the inner thighs, glutes, and quads from a slightly different angle.

Why it rocks: The farmer’s carry prepares the core for real-life activities such as carrying heavy things by your sides. It strengthens the core by making you resist the urge to bend, improving stability and balance.

Why it rocks: This exercise recruits your abdominal muscles to maintain balance and stability. A resistance band offers an added challenge for the core and lower body.

There really aren’t any exercises that are completely off-limits for older women, says Bales—as long as you’re comfortable. If an exercise causes pain, skip it. If it feels too challenging or confusing to get the hang of, try tweaking it to better suit your needs.

That said, depending on your fitness level, bone density, and current mobility and stability level, high-impact, single-side, and twisting exercises should be approached with caution, and may be best left behind for certain people, she says.

High-impact moves like jump squats and box jumps—while great for building up and strengthening your bones—put extra strain on joints, and therefore may not be a good idea for those who already experience joint pain or have arthritis, says Bales. If balance is an area of improvement for you, single-leg exercises are a great tool to rely on, as long as you’re using a stable platform to stabilize yourself and avoid ending up on the floor. Similarly, rotational exercises involving twisting of the spine are great for core strength and mobility, but can increase the risk of spinal compression fractures for those with advanced bone density issues, she says.

For beginners, it’s best to stick with slow, controlled resistance and bodyweight exercises that build strength without unnecessary strain, like bodyweight squats, resistance band work, or moderate weight lifting, says Bales. Above all, prioritize good form over the amount of weight you’re lifting, and don’t let fear stop you from getting started.

Bales’ bottom line: “Move as much as possible.” If you’re not sure which exercises are appropriate for you, consider seeing a physical therapist to get a full assessment and discuss your preferences and goals.

Building a strength training routine doesn’t have to be complicated—it just needs to be consistent. “Start small, build gradually, and stick with it,” says Bales. She recommends starting with two or three sessions per week, focusing on five to six exercises from this list for three sets of 10 reps. Try selecting an equal number of upper body, lower body, and core exercises to keep things balanced.

Progress takes time, so be patient. “Results usually show in six to eight weeks,” Bales explains. The key is to keep showing up and enjoy the process—your future self will thank you.

#5034. Fidelity files for spot Chainlink ETF with planned Nasdaq listing

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The proposed fund would hold LINK directly without staking it and is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker FLNK.

Financial services giant Fidelity has filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to launch a spot Chainlink exchange-traded fund.

The proposed Fidelity Chainlink Fund would hold LINK directly and aim to track its price, minus the fund's expenses, according to a Form S-1 filed Wednesday. The fund is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker FLNK.

LINK is the native token of Chainlink, an oracle network that helps blockchain applications access external data, such as asset prices, and communicate with other blockchains. LINK holders can also stake their tokens to earn rewards. Fidelity, however, does not plan to stake the LINK held by its proposed fund.

"The Trust will not stake its LINK, and Shareholders will not receive staking rewards through the Trust," Fidelity said in the filing.

Anchorage Digital Bank, BitGo Bank & Trust and Coinbase Custody would serve as custodians for the fund's LINK. Authorized participants would be able to create and redeem large blocks of ETF shares using either LINK or cash. The filing does not mention when the fund could begin trading.

Grayscale and Bitwise already offer U.S. spot Chainlink ETFs. As of Nov. 24, the Grayscale Chainlink Trust ETF (GLNK) had about $112 million in assets under management, and the Bitwise Chainlink ETF (CLNK) had about $42 million.

Fidelity currently offers three spot crypto ETFs in the U.S. covering bitcoin, ether, and Solana. These include the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC), the Fidelity Ethereum Fund (FETH), and the Fidelity Solana Fund (FSOL). Unlike the proposed Chainlink fund, Fidelity's Solana fund, which began trading in November 2025, stakes its tokens.

The Chainlink ETF filing comes a day after Fidelity expanded the number of cryptocurrencies available for trading on its Fidelity Crypto platform, adding Chainlink's LINK, Aave's AAVE, and Uniswap's UNI.

Fidelity also entered the stablecoin market earlier this year, launching its first U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin, Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD), on Ethereum in February.

#5033. XRP holders face a choice between earning more yield and getting their tokens back

Spectra’s February market keeps XRP-linked exposure on Flare, while getting native XRP back takes a separate redemption.

Spectra’s November XRP-linked yield pool closed on Nov. 26, and the platform is offering liquidity providers a rollover into a February Firelight market with about $1.4 million in listed liquidity.

Holders can keep their XRP-linked exposure on Flare or redeem the old position and take the separate steps to get native XRP back.

Spectra’s market overview put the Feb. 19, 2027 pool at $1.43 million and showed a 3.89% indicative fixed annual percentage yield at 10:50 UTC on Nov. 27. By 13:10 UTC, the same overview showed $1.42 million and 3.65%.

In the later snapshot, its December and March Firelight pools had $75,000 and $13,000.

Two-sided liquidity for the three Firelight stXRP maturities in Spectra’s market overview at 13:10 UTC on Nov. 27.

Source: Spectra Markets, Nov. 27 overview

The pools use stXRP, Firelight’s vault share for FXRP deposits, the version of XRP used on Flare, and Spectra pairs those shares with principal tokens that come due on a set date.

Between late Nov. 26 and the morning of Nov. 27, six transactions burned November liquidity-provider tokens and minted February pool shares for the same wallets.

The six November exits released about 27,903 stXRP, including the proceeds from redeeming the principal tokens held in the November pool.

Those rollovers deposited about 13,852 stXRP and 14,120 newly minted principal tokens into the February pool, and the rest of the stXRP went into minting those principal tokens.

A wallet redeemed 111,632 November principal tokens in a separate Flare transaction at 11:31 UTC on Nov. 27, and the transaction routed 111,138 stXRP into the February pool and sent 112,632 February principal tokens back to that wallet.

It purchased the later principal token, leaving the holder with a claim on FXRP at the new maturity.

February principal tokens can be bought at a discount and redeemed for FXRP at maturity, subject to losses in the underlying strategy.

A large order can move the price and secure a different rate, so the liquidity figure alone gives little indication of how much can trade near the displayed rate.

Spectra’s rollover review shows the quoted and worst-case fixed rates for the amount entered, plus the minimum the holder would receive. If a later market cannot offer a positive fixed rate for that amount, Spectra can exclude it and suggest a smaller order. Liquidity providers receive new February pool shares. The November rollover screen showed a 5.41% pool APY around 13:07 UTC, a variable pool return shown separately from the fixed principal-token rate. Both rollovers require the holder to act.

The February rollover keeps exposure on Flare. Returning to the XRP Ledger goes through FXRP and a separate redemption.

An exit that delivers FXRP can skip Firelight’s stXRP withdrawal window.

The 30 to 60 day window applies to direct Firelight unstaking. Market execution, redemption options, fees and payment timing vary.

Maps the outputs and actions in Spectra’s market and app guides, Firelight’s withdrawal terms, and Flare’s standard redemption procedure.

The 30 to 60 day window applies to direct Firelight unstaking. Market execution, redemption options, fees and payment timing vary.

A holder who declines to roll can redeem matured principal tokens for the default stXRP or choose FXRP when offered.

Redeeming a matured pool share first unwinds the position and redeems the principal tokens it held, with the app showing which output is available and how much the holder would receive.

Holders who receive stXRP can swap stXRP at the market price, which can differ from Firelight’s vault value, or request a direct withdrawal.

The direct route stops rewards at the request and makes FXRP claimable in 30 to 60 days under Firelight’s current coverage schedule. A second transaction collects the FXRP, and eligible claims from periods the capital backed can still reduce the payout.

FXRP received from any of those routes is still on Flare, so getting XRP back on its own ledger takes a separate FAssets redemption.

On the standard route, Flare burns the FXRP, and an agent sends native XRP to the holder’s XRP Ledger address after fees by the payment deadline. A holder who redeems directly into FXRP can go straight to that step.

Holders already able to redeem into FXRP can request native XRP without taking on a new maturity or waiting through Firelight’s unstaking window. For holders leaving with stXRP, a market swap avoids the vault’s wait if a usable quote is available.

#5030. Bitcoin miners hit by hashrate hijacking attack exploiting unencrypted connections

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Braiins is urging miners to upgrade to Stratum V2 to encrypt their connections.

Bitcoin mining pool Braiins uncovered a widespread attack that redirects bitcoin miners' hash power to steal their rewards, which it says is still ongoing.

Braiins detailed how the attack works in a Wednesday report. Bad actors are said to be exploiting a weakness in Stratum V1, a protocol used by many bitcoin miners to communicate with mining pools.

The attackers are impersonating mining pools by rerouting internet traffic, making it so miners' hashrate is being hijacked by imposters while it looks like they are mining as usual. Meanwhile, the rewards that would have been earned by the miners are instead flowing into wallets controlled by the hijackers.

Braiins identified several waves of attacks throughout November, first cropping up in Latin America before spreading to Europe. The amount of computing power being targeted grew exponentially over the span of a couple of weeks.

"The episodes so far were short, but they grew from 175 PH/s to 1.9 EH/s in two weeks, the attacker changed the method between the two waves, and it moved from one continent to another," Braiins said. "We interpret this as testing the waters."

The vulnerability has reportedly been known about for more than a decade. Braiins pointed to a 2014 incident that was originally documented by Dell SecureWorks, where an attacker used the technique to steal around $83,000 in bitcoin and other proof-of-work mining rewards over four months.

Braiins said its own systems were not compromised and that its mining pool accounts, balances and payouts were unaffected. It did not provide an estimate of the mining rewards stolen in the latest attack. It urged miners to switch to encrypted connections and the newer Stratum V2 protocol to protect themselves and their customers.

#5028. French Senate Rejects Plan to Make Crypto Holders Declare Self-Custody Wallets

French Senate Rejects Plan to Make Crypto Holders Declare Self-Custody Wallets

France's Senate has rejected a proposal that would have required crypto holders to declare self-custodied wallets worth more than €100,000 ($110,000) to tax authorities, according to the official record of Tuesday's debate on the 2027 budget.

Two identical amendments, one from the Communist-led CRCE-K group and one from a group of senators led by Anne-Sophie Romagny, were voted down after both the government and the Senate's finance committee opposed them. The vote was earlier reported by Cointelegraph.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The amendments would have obliged holders to declare self-custodied crypto above the threshold. French taxpayers already have to declare crypto accounts held on platforms, but not crypto held in their own wallets.

"The shop window is illuminated, but the back room remains in the dark," CRCE-K senator Alexandre Basquin said, in comments translated from French. The more closely platforms are monitored, the greater the incentive for large holders to keep their crypto themselves, he argued.

Minister for Public Action and Accounts David Amiel said the EU's DAC8 directive, which requires crypto service providers to report users' transactions to tax authorities, had already brought transparency. A purely declarative obligation would not let authorities track how crypto is used in money laundering or tax fraud cases, he said.

The proposal had already passed through France's lower house. The National Assembly's finance committee backed it in October, prompting a backlash from the crypto industry.

The budget was later rejected in the lower house, so the Senate is debating the government's original bill, without the crypto amendments that deputies had added.

On Tuesday, senators also rejected an amendment that would have made swaps from crypto into stablecoins a taxable event. Amiel argued that stablecoins are not money, as they have no legal tender status and are often unstable. A proposal to extend France's exit tax to crypto holdings worth more than €800,000 ($877,000) was also defeated.

Critics of the reporting plan had warned that a register of large crypto holders could become a target in France, which has become the global epicenter of "wrench attacks," in which criminals use violence to force victims to hand over crypto.

France's national anti-organized crime prosecutor's office recorded more than 70 crypto-linked kidnappings and unlawful detentions in the first eight months of 2026, Decrypt reported in September. Authorities charged 88 people, including minors, in a crackdown in April.

Leaks of personal data have added to those fears. A breach of France's tax authority in August exposed records tied to more than 678,000 people and businesses. In January, a tax agent was accused of looking up crypto investors and prison guards in tax databases for an unidentified buyer, Le Parisien reported, while a June attack in Nancy followed a data breach at French crypto tax platform Waltio.

#5026. Sens. Warren, Van Hollen lead push to scrap SEC’s Regulation Crypto and innovation exemption

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

In a letter sent to SEC Chair Atkins, Sens. Warren and Van Hollen said the agency's "Regulation Crypto Assets" would allow crypto firms to circumvent securities laws.

Top Democrats Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen are demanding that Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Paul Atkins take down its crypto rulemaking governing how crypto projects can raise capital and how tokenized securities can be traded.

In two separate letters sent to Atkins on Tuesday, Sens. Warren, Van Hollen and Tina Smith and other Senate Banking Committee members said the agency's "Regulation Crypto Assets" would allow crypto firms to circumvent securities laws, weaken state jurisdiction and could harm investors.

"The proposal would create a new 'tailored securities offering regime' for certain investment contracts involving crypto assets," the senators wrote. "However, the proposal only serves to help crypto assets escape from the SEC's regulatory regime and gives them special treatment—with less oversight—compared to other traditional securities."

In August, the SEC proposed crypto offering rules to offer startup and fundraising exemptions for digital asset offerings. It allows for a "startup exemption" that would exempt offerings of up to $5 million from registration rules under the Securities Act of 1933 for four years — a federal law focused on anti-fraud and requiring certain disclosures. The proposal also includes a "fundraising exemption" for offerings up to $75 million for a year.

Warren is poised to take on a more prominent role following Democrats’ victories in November's midterm elections, which handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Warren has been critical of crypto in the past and has particularly brought up concerns around illicit finance and money laundering. Meanwhile, Van Hollen could be the next Senate Majority Leader. He has since challenged current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for that role.

Sens. Jack Reed and Tina Smith join the two in the second letter asking the SEC to withdraw its innovation exemption — a measure released in September to bring capital markets onchain through the trading of tokenized stocks. It is a five-year exemption that would exempt certain trading venues, called tokenized securities venues, from being defined as an exchange and also exempts specific liquidity providers from being defined as a dealer under securities law when they trade stocks or provide liquidity through automated market makers.

The senators said it would allow platforms to operate outside of certain safeguards, including involving fair pricing and market transparency.

"The order would allow TSV platforms to operate a shadow stock market outside longstanding regulatory protections designed to ensure fair and transparent markets, impose new burdens on publicly traded companies seeking to protect their shareholders, and create unnecessary risks of illicit financial activity," the senators wrote.

The three senators also said the innovation exemption could cause capital markets to splinter.

"As concerned stakeholders have pointed out, fragmenting our securities markets by creating a lightly regulated alternative marketplace for tokenized securities unnecessarily risks dividing liquidity into isolated pools and expanding opportunities for corrosive regulatory arbitrage," they said.

A separate group of Senate Democrats have also brought up concerns about the innovation exemption. Last week, Sens. Angela Alsobrooks, Ruben Gallego, Mark Warner and Catherine Cortez Masto said it could open the door for illicit finance actors and also had concerns about protections for retail investors around pricing.

Even if you pride yourself on eating whole foods and cooking healthy meals, it can still be super hard to get all of the vitamins and minerals your body needs. Plus, your nutrient needs change as you age.

For instance, “as women navigate through the wonderful world of the menopause transition, there are changes, health-wise, that happen,” says Leslie Bonci, RD, a sports dietitian based in Pittsburgh. As your hormone levels start to decrease, you may be more likely to lose bone density and muscle mass. When these changes happen, “there are certain nutrients that are going to be needed more than others,” she adds. That’s when it can be helpful to turn to a supplement.

Meet the experts: Leslie Bonci, RD, is a sports dietitian based in Pittsburgh. Navya Mysore, MD, is a primary care physician, women's health expert, and WH advisory board member based in New York City.

Knowing which supplements you should take in each stage of life may be complicated, but we found the right experts to simplify everything. Consider this your supplement roadmap.

First, have a conversation with your primary care physician—they should know about all of the medications and supplements you’re currently taking or are considering. Your doc will help you ensure supplementation is the best course of action after considering your holistic health care plan. Then, they can rule out any potential medication interactions and decide which dosage is best, says Navya Mysore, MD, a primary care physician, women's health expert, and WH advisory board member based in New York City.

Here are some of the most common interactions, per Dr. Mysore and Bonci:

You also might want to get blood work done before starting a supplement, especially if you think you may have a deficiency. “Checking things like iron stores (ferritin), vitamin D, or B12 can tell you if you actually need a supplement and how much,” says Dr. Mysore. However, you don’t need blood work if you’re just taking a basic prenatal or multivitamin.

Just remember: “Supplements are a complement to—not a replacement for—eating,” Bonci says. They’re just one piece of the puzzle; in order to live your healthiest, longest, best life, you’ll want to make sure you’re eating nutritiously and exercising consistently.

Sorry to our gummy lovers out there: “Capsules usually win—they tend to absorb better and have fewer fillers,” says Dr. Mysore. “Tablets are fine but a bit more variable.” Unfortunately, gummies are often underdosed and may not include key nutrients like iron, she adds. So, your safest bet is a capsule.

#5022. Morning Minute: Ethereum Focuses on Security As AI Threats Rise

Morning Minute: Ethereum Focuses on Security As AI Threats Rise

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

The Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and made cryptography its top priority. The reason isn’t quantum computers.

Protocol lead Kev Wedderburn wrote this week that “recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk”, and the distinction matters. The quantum threat has always been a hardware problem, and hardware problems announce themselves years in advance because somebody has to build the machine. The AI version is a math problem. A sufficiently capable model could find a structural shortcut in the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin, and it would need no special hardware to do it.

Researcher Justin Drake raised the scenario in October. In a worst case, he said, existing signatures could become vulnerable within months.

An Anthropic mathematician named Levent Alpöge posted a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, produced with an unreleased version of Claude, along with a formalized proof archive. Nobody has verified it. It doesn’t break elliptic curve cryptography and nobody is claiming it does. What it does is demonstrate the capability class Drake was describing, roughly a month after he described it.

Axios reported Tuesday that more than two dozen people familiar with internal discussions at OpenAI and Anthropic say employees worry their most advanced unreleased models may never be safe enough to release. The concerns named include reward hacking, models that hide or misrepresent their reasoning, and systems capable enough to find weaknesses in the safety measures their own developers built. OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed Sunday that labs agree on shared limits on how far they train models.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The plan replaces elliptic curves with hash-based cryptography, which rests on fewer structural assumptions about mathematics. It touches how users authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how layer-2 data gets verified. Drake proposed pulling the deadline from December 2029 to December 2028. Ethlabs withdrew its faster-block-production proposal from the Hegotá upgrade to free up engineers. The Foundation has deployed AI agents to hunt bugs in its own infrastructure, which is a reasonable response and also an admission about where the advantage currently sits.

Wedderburn’s own framing: it’s harder than the Merge, and there’s less time. He also acknowledged that moving faster makes it easier to ship bugs.

Bitcoin is on the same road. Blockstream’s Jonas Nick published a security analysis of SHRINCS last week, the apparent frontrunner to replace Bitcoin’s signatures, with sizes running from 548 bytes to 5,777 against today’s 64 to 71.

So the AI threat is looming (and accelerating), but the two largest crypto assets have teams that are responding. Now we wait on action, and more assurances that crypto is safe from AI threats. Assurances that could ensure the bottom is in fact in, if and when they arrive…

#5021. LayerZero adds Samsung Card, Kakao Pay, ZAN as validators for upcoming Zero blockchain

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

LayerZero Co-founder and CEO Bryan Pellegrino said the additions of Asian financial institutions are meant to give Zero a more globally distributed set of validators from the start.

LayerZero LayerZero (ZRO) has named Kakao Pay, Samsung Card, and ZAN as new validators for Zero, its blockchain network expected to launch on Nov. 30.

The three will join the upcoming mainnet as genesis validators and help secure the network's consensus and proof-verification system at launch. Four Pillars, a South Korean blockchain research firm, will operate the validator node on behalf of Samsung Card.

Samsung Card, a subsidiary of South Korea's largest conglomerate, had approximately 13.92 million cardholders as of the end of September. KakaoPay, linked with the country's largest mobile messaging app, has roughly 26 million monthly users. ZAN is the Web3 infrastructure platform backed by Ant Digital Technologies that provides node services across more than 80 chains.

LayerZero co-founder and CEO Bryan Pellegrino said the additions of Asian financial heavyweights are meant to give Zero a more globally distributed set of validators from the start.

"The future of global markets needs Better Markets Technology: infrastructure that matches not only the speed and borderless nature of tokenized assets, but the structural resilience of globally distributed ecosystems," Pellegrino said. "We're thrilled to partner with some of Asia's most influential financial services firms to bring that vision to life with a truly global set of validators."

The Layer 1 blockchain is designed primarily for institutional and global financial markets. Unlike most blockchains that re-execute every transaction, the chain uses ZK proofs to separate execution from verification, removing a layer of redundancy by leaving validators to only verify the proofs, LayerZero said.

Zero is scheduled to go live on Nov. 30 alongside LayerZero's ATLAS trading infrastructure. Staked ZRO will be distributed equally across genesis validators until March 31, 2027.

Kakao Pay CEO Shin Won-keun said the company plans to explore the Zero network to bridge traditional finance and onchain markets, including initiatives based on stablecoins pegged to the South Korean won.
