#5020. Bitcoin Has Become Boring, Finally

Bitcoin isn't a shiny new technology any more, it is established, and it is here to stay.

The 2019 Lightning conference in Berlin was lit: five hundred “cypherpunks” getting each other high on visions of a future with peer-to-peer electronic cash. Attending a bitcoin conference back in the day felt like being a teenager at a friend’s party while their parents were out of town. It was exciting and new. The feeling was the opposite of FOMO: something big was happening, we were on the inside, and the rest of the world was going to envy us. It was the kind of party that you could only have when the adults weren’t looking. Whenever someone bought a beer (with bitcoin), everyone would hoot and holler and record it on their phones for Instagram/Twitter (it was still called Twitter).

Lightning was the bleeding edge. We called it “the Lightning Network” (capitalized, if you please), and talking about it felt like talking about string theory: something so far out you’re not even sure it’s real. I spent a lot of time invoking the abacus.

Those are the times some of us remember fondly and keep trying to relive at bitcoin conferences today. That’s why we engage in rituals like drone shows, Satoshi Rockamoto sets, beefsteak dinners, and video game tournaments for sats, but it’s not the same. The ratio of bitcoin OG speakers to suits is shifting. Many event rooms are half empty, and the halls and meeting rooms are full of people negotiating cap tables and profit-sharing splits.

The adults haven’t shut the party down, but they have crashed it, and it kinda feels like their party now. The most exciting thing I noticed at the last bitcoin conference I attended was that nothing exciting happened.

The road to boring is seldom smooth. Technological innovation benefits from passion and bold ideas. People work harder on a project when they feel strongly about it and identify closely with like-minded collaborators. That’s where tech subcultures, their rituals, and their dogmas come from. But such passion and tribalism feed conflict, at least for a while until the tech goes mainstream, and normies, who couldn’t care less about subculture squabbles, take over.

This progression from an exciting new technology that inspires strong emotions to a humdrum utility is not unusual. World-changing innovations often (always?) start with a committed subculture that identifies fiercely with their weird tech before the mainstream adopts it and soon expects it. In fact, this trajectory has become the standard doctrine of tech marketing. For example, in the early days of the internet, early adopters wrote a Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, picking a fight with states and corporations despite having nothing to back it up but chatrooms and dreams.

One case that resembles the early days of bitcoin was the war of the currents between high-voltage AC current and low-voltage DC current in the 1880s-1890s. Both featured big personalities stunning audiences with flashy demos at conferences. Edison and Westinghouse wowed crowds with their lightbulbs that made artificial light, just like bitcoiners in 2019 wowed YouTube by buying beer with bitcoin. And both cases featured rabid subcultures that accused each other of putting the future of the technology, if not of humanity, at stake. In the 1880s, the issue was whether AC was more deadly to humans and animals than DC; in the 2010s it was whether limiting the size of bitcoin’s blocks to 1MB would perpetuate monetary servitude forever.

In both cases, there were devoted subcultures whose disagreements helped the technology to mature before the tech crossed the chasm of exoticism to become the new, boring normal. Both are now largely managed by experts on pragmatic principles, not passionate conviction. Conferences went from spectacular showcases for technological miracles to sedate affairs where professionals debate and agree on industry standards. Pragmatism and consensus replaced ideology and dissent. In both instances things got boring, and boring was actually better.

Bitcoin is getting boring, although what that means and how it’s come to be that way depends on your point of view. As always, where you stand depends on where you sit.

Generally speaking, there are two broad points of view on what bitcoin is and is for. And though they started in different places, they’re both coming to a common conclusion: bitcoin is more boring than ever. So let’s review these two points of view, how they view bitcoin now, and why both would agree that the status quo is now so awfully, wonderfully boring.

The basic existential question that defined bitcoin’s first decade is settled: bitcoin is not a scam, and it’s not going away. That status is stable largely because bitcoin is now too big to fail, with a market cap exceeding a trillion dollars.

Much of this scale is thanks to the millions of people who want to own bitcoin as part of their savings, but not necessarily to trade and circulate it. In other words, they see bitcoin as a better form of gold, not cash. These savers want to integrate bitcoin into their fiat portfolio, just like any other asset. They aren’t terribly concerned about bitcoin’s status as a medium of exchange so long as it becomes firmly established as a viable, tradable commodity.

People investing in bitcoin are happy when the number goes up, and it generally does (you might have to zoom out on the price graph a bit, depending on the week). Bitcoin used to be a rollercoaster; now it’s more of a hike. The ups and downs still happen, but they’re gentler and a bit more predictable. How boring.

Bitcoin’s price started to settle down as mainstream finance started growing more comfortable with it as an asset. Whereas conventional finance used to want governments to shut bitcoin down, there is now about $100B worth of bitcoin held in ETFs and traded on ordinary equity markets. Major banks used to shun bitcoin, and now they accept it as collateral. Bitcoin is a regular feature in corporate treasuries, and some companies exist just to hold bitcoin. Strategy is worth about $55B on the open market, and it holds about $63B worth of bitcoin, so the entire company is a discounted bitcoin wallet. Bitcoin is also a regular feature in retirement accounts, pension allocations, and sovereign wealth funds. Thinking of bitcoin as another kind of asset ripe for institutional and retail investors now makes a lot of sense, because that’s what it is.

Why are these canny investors bored? It seems that all the exciting developments leading to bitcoin becoming a valuable asset have already happened. If the goal was integration into the world of conventional finance, it has incontrovertibly been achieved. You can’t YOLO on bitcoin any more than you can YOLO on gold. The milestones are all in the history section of the Wikipedia page, not on the roadmap.

People who wanted bitcoin to become a tradable asset are bored because mainstream finance has effectively tamed bitcoin. It is easily tradable, and its trading volumes are remarkable. It is digital gold, just with a slightly steeper curve and a little more volatility, which is exactly what these folks always wanted.

The main alternative to seeing bitcoin as a mainstream investment asset is to view it as monetary dynamite to ignite a revolution. People subscribing to this point of view wanted bitcoin to blossom into a system of peer-to-peer electronic cash that would first operate in parallel to the mainstream monetary system before supplanting it. These radicals wanted to see the banks collapse, not accept bitcoin as collateral. It was monetary insurrection, not incremental change.

This radical point of view is still around, but the wind has gone out of its combative sails for a few reasons.

First, there has been a generational shift. Many of the people who were pushing the revolutionary vision of bitcoin in their 20s fifteen years ago have moved on. Some got rich and retired or started to see and use bitcoin more as a tradable asset. For others, bitcoin never achieved the success they dreamt of, but it was successful enough that fighting for its future no longer felt necessary.

Second, AI is the new cool kid on the tech block. Instead of building vending machines for beer that accept bitcoin, enthusiasts who want to hack the system are now decompiling games with AI. No VC will waste a second on a pitch deck that doesn’t have AI on at least half of the slides. Miners are turning their server stacks and power contracts into AI data centers. Curious engineers have a new, much bigger toy to play with.

Third, mainstream bitcoin fans on Wall Street simply consume too much bandwidth. Not surprisingly, banks, publicly traded companies, and financial institutions with billions in their pockets are dominating panels at conferences and supplying the talking heads for financial news shows. They want to discuss topics like volatility and discount rates instead of personal sovereignty and individual financial freedom. Fighting against the system is not a narrative they can sell while representing the interests of that very system.

Fourth, bitcoin usage has moved past the radical mantras and progressed in a different direction. The dream of bitcoin becoming the standard payment medium in a circular economy where everyone buys coffee with bitcoin (why is it always coffee?) is starting to feel like an alternative history in a parallel universe.

A circular economy is simply not the role in society bitcoin has grown into. Instead of everyday payments, bitcoin is the medium of global value transfer. It has evolved into a technology to move real money across borders as remittances, into a settlement layer between various crypto assets, and into a store of value that people constantly buy, sell, and trade. It’s become a valuable network of rails that even stablecoins are happy to use.

Fixating on coffee purchases obscures the remarkable scale bitcoin has achieved. Somewhere between $1.6 and $4.1 trillion was settled on-chain between Q1 and Q3 2026 (depending on how you count). PayPal processed $1.79 trillion in all of 2025. The average payment on PayPal is about $70. The average bitcoin transaction (using the strict counting method) is $10,000. With bitcoin moving trillions in value, we can stop worrying about coffee.

Bitcoin may not have cornered retail payments, but it’s a mature and highly liquid asset. It’s an industry unto itself. It has found its place in the economy, and it’s thriving. Despite the lack of revolutionary fireworks, bitcoin is changing mainstream finance by opening new possibilities and financially enfranchising new user groups. That’s still worth celebrating.

You know what’s really boring? Electricity infrastructure. You know what no one can live without despite how boring it is? Electricity infrastructure.

When revolutionary technologies fade into the background of everyday life, when people use them constantly without thinking about them, they become boring, and they become essential. Buying a beer with Lightning is no longer exciting because we can now expect that it will just work without fanfare. Being able to say “it will just work” sounds boring, but it’s a clear sign of triumph.

Bitcoiners and builders need to adjust to this beautiful, boring reality. We can stop annoying our neighbors with orange pills. It’s about utility, not evangelism. Utility means building rails that bitcoin and stablecoins can use together seamlessly, adding bitcoin to mainstream fintech apps, and building new financial applications on top of the bitcoin chain. Perhaps none of this will light the fireworks at the radicals’ victory party or replace T-bills as the base layer of global finance, but every user who discovers the unique utility of bitcoin is further evidence of its mainstream adoption.

What we have is a thriving technology that enables us to do miraculous new things, and it’s achieved an undeniable scale, such that it is now too big to fail. That’s fantastic. It may not be the future we were dreaming about seven years ago in Berlin, but it’s wonderful in its own right, and it’s worth cultivating and celebrating.

Even though nobody sets out to grow up and become boring one day, it’s still a valid kind of success. It means you’ve made it, and you’re doing fine. Boring is what happens when things just work and things have just worked out. So we didn’t break the world with bitcoin. Oh well. We’re making a new one. A party with adults present is still a party. And maybe we’re now the adults. So dance while you wait for the dollar to collapse 😉

#5019. House Committee advances Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill with narrow path to passage

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The current 119th Congress is expected to adjourn in the coming weeks, leaving little time for a House floor vote, Senate consideration, and final passage before the session ends.

The House Financial Services Committee has advanced H.R. 8957, the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, which would codify a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and impose a minimum 20-year lock on federally held bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC).

The legislation, introduced on May 21 by Rep. Nick Begich, would allow the Treasury secretary to establish a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a separate Digital Asset Stockpile for other cryptocurrencies 180 days after enactment.

Once deposited in the reserve, bitcoin cannot be "sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of for any purpose" for at least 20 years. The bill also includes transparency requirements such as proof-of-reserve reporting and directs federal agencies to report existing holdings.

On Sept. 16, the House Financial Services Committee approved it on a party-line vote of 28-21, with support from every Republican representative and opposition from every Democrat. On Nov. 24, the committee officially sent the revised bill to the full House, where it is now eligible for a floor vote.

The bill builds on U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order issued in March 2025 that directed the creation of a bitcoin reserve funded mainly through bitcoin already owned by the government from criminal or civil forfeitures, and a separate digital asset stockpile. The order sparked concern from some lawmakers on bitcoin's riskiness and volatility.

While the bill is now on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 789, its chances of passing are low. The current 119th Congress is expected to adjourn in the coming weeks, leaving little time for a House floor vote, Senate consideration, and final passage before the session ends.

Polymarket odds show a 4% chance of the U.S. establishing a national bitcoin reserve by the end of this year, down from 60% around a year ago and 34% in May this year.

If the bill fails to pass within this Congress, it would have to be reintroduced in the 120th Congress. The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve created by the March 2025 executive order would remain in place, but a future president could alter or reverse it without congressional approval. Reintroducing and advancing the initiative may face steeper challenges as Democrats are set to control both chambers starting in January.

#5018. 16 Best Strength Training Exercises to Build Muscle and Strength Fast

There’s no shortage of strength training exercises to pepper into your muscle-building routine. If you’re a regular on FitTok, you might’ve noticed that a new exercise seems to pop up regularly. So, which ones should you pepper into your routine?

“It all comes down to your goal,” says Angela Gargano, a trainer and creator of Strong Feels Good & Pull-up Revolution. The exercises you fill your program with are your most important tools for success.

Keep reading for the best strength training exercises to try, exactly how to add them into a total-body routine, and expert-backed tips for making a plan that works. Ready to get lifting?

Build lasting strength with the WH+ Strong Over 50 Plan, here

Below, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite strength training exercises, spanning all the different muscle groups. Here’s how to create a well-rounded full-body routine you can do regularly.

Equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebell, resistance band | Good for: Total body Instructions: Pick one move from each category—push, pull, hinge, lunge, squat—to create a total body workout. Do it two to three days a week, preferably on nonconsecutive days. For each move, do the allocated amount of sets and reps, resting for 1 to 2 minutes between sets. Select weights that make the last few reps challenging, but doable (and more on selecting weights, below!).

Alternatively, you can split up muscle groups if you have multiple days a week to work out (if you’re working out only two days a week or less, stick with a full-body plan). There are a few ways to do this. If you're planning on strength training twice a week, you can also opt to do one upper-body day (the push/pull exercises) and one lower-body day (the hinge/lunge/squat exercises). Select four or five exercises with a variety of exercise type (don’t fill a lower body day with only squats, no matter how much you love them!) to create your workout.

Or, if you're working out three times a week, you can split your workouts to do one push/pull day, and two hinge/lunge/squat days, or vice versa, depending on what part of your body you want to strengthen most. If you're training more than three times a week, you can split by muscle group.

Here are 16 of the best strength training exercises to fill in your workout.

Why it rocks: Pushups are a classic move for a reason: They work your chest, shoulders, and triceps. Another perk? They engage your core muscles and build functional strength.

Why it rocks: This is an excellent bent-over row variation that targets your lats and rhomboids, requiring less core stability than a traditional bent-over row.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Deadlifts build overall strength and power in the posterior chain muscles, including the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back.

Why it rocks: Reverse lunges work the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes, all while improving coordination and stability.

Why it rocks: Curtsy lunges torch the glutes and outer thighs, while also improving lower body strength and muscle symmetry.

Strength training can help you build and maintain muscle mass, improve your joint and bone health, support better body composition, and even increase your longevity. And, including it in your routine is easy to do, as long as you follow these tips and tricks.

“The biggest thing in putting together your entire workout is making sure that you have a proper warm-up, always, no matter what,” says Gargano. “People tend to throw that out the window but dynamic moves are going to help you wake the body up a little bit before you get into your strength training.”

To execute a proper warm-up, select 3 to 4 dynamic and mobility exercises (these are a few of our favorites!) and do them for 30 seconds apiece, 2 or 3 times through. If you're planning on exercising a specific part of your body that day, make sure your warm-up is tailored to that (e.g., if you're about to do a leg day lift, select a few warm-up moves that promote blood flow to the lower body, like lateral lunges or the World's Greatest Stretch).

“In your programming, there’s a combination of things you should always have,” says Gargano, noting you don’t have to put them all in the same workout/day, but they should certainly all fit in your week: Push movements (like pushups and chest presses), pull movements (like pull-ups and rows), squats, lunges, and hinge movements (think: deadlifts, hip hinges).

Programming your workouts will largely depend on how many times a week you work out (more on that here). The more times a week you can exercise, the more you can split your workouts by muscle group. For example, if you're working out three days per week, you might be interested in doing one upper-body day, one leg day focused on glutes and hamstrings, and another focused on quads and calves. If you're only working out twice per week, you'll want to make sure you're programming for the whole body: at least one upper-body lift and one lower-body lift.

“I know people are going to be like, ‘Well, what about my core?’ but your core is used in all those movements,” Gargano assures.

“You want to be sure that you're working all the body parts so that you're not uneven,” says Gargano. It's an issue trainers see a lot—people focus so hard on defining one part of their body that they neglect the rest. For example, if you're aiming to build up your glutes, don't only do hip thrusts on lower body day. Incorporate some lunges and squats in there, too, to strengthen your quad muscles so they can work in tandem with your strong glutes.

As long as you hit all five of the main movement patterns we named earlier (push, pull, squat, lunge, hip hinge) throughout the week, you should be in good shape.

A few weeks into your workout program, your body will get used to what you’re doing—so you'll need to level up the challenge, “so that your body can continue to develop and work the muscles in different ways,” says Gargano. That means increasing your weights, reps, or sets to progressively overload the muscles—doing so will help them get continuously stronger, and ensure your performance never plateaus.

To know when to up the weights, use the two-for-two rule: Once you can do two extra good-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load. From there, try to increase 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. But remember, this is just a recommendation—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

The best exercise plan is the one you're going to stick to. And the one you're going to stick to is the one that best fits into your schedule.

“You need to figure out what is working well for you and your body,” says Gargano. “Everybody's different, so try out two days a week first, and then if you feel good, maybe add that third day.”

Once you have your schedule set, don't feel like it's an end-all, be-all. The more you can hit your workouts, the better—but there's no reason to knock yourself down if things get busy and you miss one or two. You can always abbreviate your workout by cutting a few exercises or sets, or get moving by going for a brief walk. The key is to stay moving as much as you can. It won't always be perfect, and that's okay.

Ukraine's parliament has passed a law to legalize the country's crypto market and tax virtual asset transactions, with the new rules set to take effect on July 1, 2027.

The Verkhovna Rada approved bill No. 10225-d in its second reading and as a whole on Wednesday, with 271 lawmakers voting in favor, Yaroslav Zhelezniak, first deputy chair of the parliament's finance, tax and customs committee, said on Telegram. The law still needs to be signed by President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Zhelezniak said the law would bring in an extra 15 billion hryvnias (around $330 million) in budget revenue.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Under the law, individuals will pay 18% personal income tax and a 5% military levy on profits from crypto transactions, according to state news agency Ukrinform. Swapping one crypto asset for another will not be taxed, and losses from previous years can be carried forward.

For crypto bought before the law takes effect, a reduced rate will apply when holders cash out into traditional currency during 2027 and 2028: 5% plus the military levy. Zhelezniak wrote that the reduced rate would apply to "the entire volume," rather than only to profits.

Oversight will be split between the National Securities and Stock Market Commission and the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU). The central bank will be responsible for stablecoins, and can set its own rules for their use, including allowing or banning their circulation.

The NBU will also authorize and supervise issuers of e-money tokens and providers that exchange virtual assets for traditional money, the central bank said in a statement, according to Interfax-Ukraine.

Ukraine first moved to legalize crypto in 2021, and Zelensky signed a law on virtual assets in March 2022, weeks after Russia's full-scale invasion. Soon after, the NBU banned purchases of crypto with hryvnias.

The new bill, which adds tax rules and aligns Ukraine's regulation more closely with the EU's as part of its bid for membership, passed its first reading in September 2025.

Ukraine has also explored other ways to bring crypto into the state's orbit. Lawmakers submitted a bill to create a strategic crypto reserve in June 2025, and in June 2026, the country placed more than $8.3 million in seized USDT under state management for the first time.

#5014. Galaxy walks back bitcoin’s June-bottom call, warns of deeper losses below $58,525

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Galaxy now treats a daily close below $58,525, the June 30 closing low, as the start of a move toward a materially lower low.

Galaxy has withdrawn its October call that bitcoin's bear market ended in June, warning that the world's largest cryptocurrency could move even lower when it breaks the June level.

In a research note released Wednesday, Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, wrote that the team's previous technical argument is "no longer valid" and that the team now treats a daily close below $58,525 — the June 30 closing low — as the start of a move toward a materially lower low.

Galaxy's revised outlook comes as the crypto market remained volatile. Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) rose 2.4% over the past 24 hours to trade at $60,677 as of 10:50 p.m. ET Wednesday, after falling to as low as around $57,300 earlier in the day, according to The Block's BTC price page. Ethereum Ethereum (ETH) climbed 2.1% to $1,695, BNB gained 3.2%, and XRP added 4.2%.

Last month, Thorn had suggested that bitcoin's bear market ended in June. He cited Galaxy's September reclaim of the 50-week moving average, a level that has historically served as a ceiling during bear markets. However, Thorn's latest note points out that after seven weekly closes above the average, bitcoin closed back below it in early November and later closed below the 200-week average.

"[Although] bitcoin has until about Dec. 8 to regain the average, we must acknowledge that the bear market is very likely not over and that the reclaim is unlikely to come in time," Thorn said in the note. "Previously, no reclaim of this kind had been followed by a new low."

Galaxy said that a daily close below $58,525 would be a "break of a standing low," adding that in all seven prior bear markets when bitcoin broke a similar standing low, the prices fell at least another 17%.

The firm also noted that the macro backdrop has deteriorated since June. On Nov. 19, the two-year Treasury yield was 0.88 percentage point above the fed funds rate — "a sign that the market is pricing a higher policy rate ahead," Thorn said. Also, the S&P 500 was 1.5% below its record at the June low and closed 11.6% below it on Nov. 20, according to the report.

U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded products have shed 71,339 BTC ($4.95 billion) since Oct. 4, with outflows on 22 of 35 sessions, according to Galaxy. That left holdings at an estimated 1.24 million BTC, 9.7% below the Oct. 9, 2025, peak.

"Whether Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia on Nov. 23 can be the spark that pulls bitcoin back up to levels needed to end the bear market is unknown," Thorn added.

Thorn said traders should watch whether bitcoin can hold its June lows of $58,525 on a daily close and $59,517 on a weekly closing basis. "A weekly close back above the 200-week average, then the 50-week average, would bring us back toward our October view," Thorn said.

Beyond the technical levels, the firm is also watching whether financial advisors increase their bitcoin ETP holdings and whether the two-year Treasury yield moves back toward the fed funds rate.

#5012. Lifting Heavy Isn’t the Whole Story When It Comes to Building Strength. Here's What to Do Instead.

My name is Cori Ritchey, and I am an exercise physiology nerd turned fitness journalist, and the fitness editor at Women’s Health. When I’m not writing, editing, and researching fitness, I’m teaching it to my personal training and group fitness clients. In my new column, Between Sets, I’m pulling back the curtain on the same advice, tips, and ‘aha!’ moments I share with my clients while they’re catching their breath. Stick around for the strategic, science-backed nuggets that’ll help you move better, train smarter, and actually enjoy the process.

Scroll any fitness feed and you’ll see it: people clanging plates, chasing PRs, and even pulling dangerous stunts for the pride of lifting heavy. And where there’s real joy in getting stronger, there’s also real pressure to keep adding weight.

As a strength and conditioning coach and the fitness editor at Women’s Health, I’ve been preaching the lift-heavy-or-go-home gospel for years. For valid reason: challenging your muscles over time is one of the most reliable ways to build lasting strength, support bone health, improve body composition, and stay functional as we age.

The “lift heavy” ethos isn’t new. Strength training is as old as Ancient Greece, where the first gyms were developed. It progressed through decades of physical culture into Muscle Beach, USA, the birthplace of American lifting that started as a beachside gymnastics park in Venice Beach, California, in the 1940s. It was there, too, where the first American women bodybuilders, like legendary Abbey Stockton, emerged—at a time when many scientists still believed lifting was bad for the body.

Research eventually caught up to what lifters were already experiencing: resistance training works. More women, especially in recent years, started showing up for it, too. In 2004, 17 percent of women reported regularly participating in weight lifting. By 2020, that number has bumped to nearly 30 percent. Then came the influencer era, amplifying a message that’s equal parts motivating and misleading: lifting weights is good for you—but it has to be heavy to count.

There’s a kernel of truth in there. Progressive overload (the process of gradually increasing the stress you put on your body in a workout) builds muscle and strength, and increasing load is an efficient way to do so.

And that matters—especially when heavier, heavier, heavier simply isn’t in the cards.

Because for many, it’s not. It requires access to specific equipment, time to train consistently without rushing through sets, and quality coaching and information to nail form and stay injury-free. It also has to be safe and appropriate for your body on any given day—whether you’re navigating chronic illness, postpartum or perimenopause realities, and injury history, or limiting pain. And even when everything lines up on paper, there’s a very real mental hurdle: walking into a gym and loading up a bar can be intimidating as hell.

Still, if you’re here to build strength, change your body composition, protect your bone health, or invest in your movement longevity, lifting heavier will certainly help—but it’s not the only path to lifelong strength. Somewhere along the way, “heavy” became synonymous with “effective”, and “light” or "moderate" became codes for “waste of time.”

The exercise research world is finding that’s not the case. “You don't need to do anything heavy for the health benefits of resistance exercise to take place,” says Stuart Phillips, PhD, kinesiology professor and hypertrophy researcher at McMaster University.

Adequate research has suggested that hypertrophy (the fancy scientific term for muscle growth) is not determined by a magic rep goal or the weight on the bar, says Susie Reiner, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, assistant professor of exercise science at Seton Hall University, and CEO of TheoryEx, a sport science research and consulting firm. “Instead, hypertrophy appears to be driven by whether a training set provides a sufficiently strong internal stimulus to the muscle, which is reasonably defined as effort and proximity to muscular failure.”

Trainers have traditionally been taught that specific rep ranges map neatly to specific goals: 1 to 3 for power, 3 to 8 for strength, 8 to 12 for muscle, and 12-plus for muscular endurance. But newer findings show you can build muscle across a much wider rep range—roughly as low as 5 and as high as 25, Phillips says. “There is, then, by definition, no sweet spot for muscle building, because the whole repetition range then becomes the sweet spot.”

Across several studies and meta-analyses, similar muscle growth has been seen between people who train with lighter loads (about 30 to 40 percent of their one-rep maximum), and those who train with heavier loads (about 70 to 85 percent of their one-rep maximum)—as long as sets are taken close enough to failure.

Muscle growth is dependent on recruiting and fatiguing a large portion of muscle fibers, Reiner says. Your muscles need a reason to adapt. With heavier weights for fewer reps, you recruit a lot of fibers immediately. With lighter weights for higher reps, you recruit them more gradually.

One thing to note here: while a large percentage of these studies have only been done in men, Phillips notes that “the work that has been done in women shows us that actually men and women respond very, very similarly to weight lifting in terms of muscle mass gain. Women have less baseline muscle, but relatively speaking, they gain the same amount as men—that's been robustly shown.” Phillips and his colleagues are currently running several studies (including one study specific to perimenopausal women!) that will further clarify what this looks like in women.

Researchers feel confident that as long as sets are taken sufficiently to failure (more on what that means coming up), different loading strategies can produce similar hypertrophy, Reiner says.

Here’s what that looks like IRL: Let’s say you have biceps curls on your workout plan each week. One week, you pick up the 10-pound dumbbells, and do 3 sets of 12 reps. In the sets, when you approach the end of that rep range, it feels tough—you can maybe grind out 2 more reps max. The next week, you reach for the 15s. You can only hit 6 reps before you feel like your form is faltering, but the effort feels similar—you’ve still got about two reps left before your form breaks down.

The heavier weight might feel more empowering, but both workouts deliver a similar muscle-building stimulus—assuming you’re training regularly enough, eating enough protein and calories, and adequately recovering, of course.

Sure, research confirms you don’t have to lift crazy heavy—but that doesn’t mean that coming close to failure feels easy. Failing a rep can be scary (and honestly, discouraging). Here’s the good news: you don’t need true, all-out failure. You just need to train to proximity to failure.

One practical way to gauge that is with the rate of perceived exertion scale. “Rate of perceived exertion (RPE) is a global effort scale, typically ranging from one to 10,” Reiner says. An RPE of 10 represents maximal effort—no chance you could do one more rep. A RPE of nine suggests you could do one more, an RPE of eight means you could probably do two more reps, and so on and so forth.

Muscle growth still occurs between RPE of 7 to 9, Phillips says. “You don’t need it to be a 10 out of 10 where you’re red-lining and can’t get the bar off your chest.” In other words: you can train hard without routinely hitting the point where things get sketchy.

That matters, because the closer you get to all-out failure, the more your injury risk can creep up—especially if you start twisting, bouncing, and compensating to force a rep you simply don’t have.

The failure you want to flirt with is technical failure, or technical fatigue. “Technical failure means you cannot complete another repetition with good form,” Phillips says—that’s where injury risk rises. Muscular failure (otherwise known as momentary failure) occurs when a muscle is unable to generate enough force to complete another rep, regardless of maximal effort. Picture trying to do one more biceps curl and you quite literally cannot lift your arm and the weight up again—that’s muscular failure..

Aim for technical failure. Pushing yourself too far in an effort to achieve muscular failure could cause your body to overcompensate and push you into a compromising position. The good news, too, is technical failure tends to be very close to muscular failure for most people, Phillips says.

A useful rule of thumb: stop when you have one to two perfect-form reps left in the tank.

Yes, you still need to reach for that RPE of 7 to 9—but there’s more ways to do that than just reaching for the next highest weight. Here are some other elements you can play with to up the challenge:

Frequency. Reaching for heavier weights, you can simply aim to reach for any type of weight more often. That might look like increasing your strength training days from two to three days a week.

Volume. Think of your training volume as the amount of weight total you lift during a given session. Sure, lifting heavier loads is one way to increase your total, but it can also be accomplished by increasing the amount of sets or reps you do.

Rest time. Decreasing the amount of rest you allow yourself gives your muscles less time to recover, wearing them out quicker with lighter loads.

Time under tension. The amount of time your muscles work for matters. Increasing your time under tension, or the amount of time your muscles are working in a lift (for example, lowering a curl for a slow four-count).

That all being said, heavier loads might still take the cake in terms of efficiency. You’ll find yourself increasing your frequency and volume to monotonous levels if you never increase your load.

Back to biceps curls: Say you get comfortable at six reps at 15 lbs. After a few weeks, it no longer starts to feel challenging for you, so you increase it eight. And then 10. And then 12. If you never reach for the intimidating 20 lb dumbbells, you’ll eventually find yourself having to do sets of 30 reps just to feel something. And that can become time consuming. You don’t need extremes all the time—but you do need your training to stay challenging.

“For individuals who are uncomfortable training to very high levels of effort, consistent training at moderate-to-high RPEs combined with sufficient volume and progression can still produce meaningful muscle growth,” Reiner says. “From a long-term perspective, hypertrophy depends less on any single maximal set and more on repeated exposure to challenging, well-managed training over weeks and months.”

Convinced to start pushing closer to failure? Here are a few ways to progress safely.

The two-for-two method is a classic progression strategy used by professional trainers. Once you can do two extra proper-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load.

Let's use the biceps curl example just one more time. You’ve been training with the 15s for sets of 8, and now you can hit 10 with clean form for two workouts in a row. That’s your cue to grab 17.5s the next go.

How much should you increase, exactly? The National Strength and Conditioning Association’s guideline is 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. Reminder that this is just a general guide—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

Trying heavier weights is way less intimidating when you have a safety net.

If you’re nervous, ask for a spot. Maybe you already have a gym buddy you workout with regularly that can help pull the barbell up if you get stuck on a bench press. If you don’t, ask one of your gym’s trainers or employees. Most people will politely oblige, and will even appreciate your effort in challenging yourself.

Have a conversation with your spotter before you get into the lift. Tell them how many reps you’re aiming for, and a cue you’ll give them when you want them to jump in and help (my go-to is a simple “now”—since that’s about all you can get out when you’re out of breath).

Some days just don’t feel as strong as others. Maybe you didn’t sleep super well last night, stressed about work, or are at a tough point in your cycle. That’s life. When that happens, you need to respect the cues your body gives you.

If your warmup sets feel unusually heavy, take the hint: this just might not be the day to pick up that heavy weight. It doesn’t mean you’ve regressing, it’s just a bump in the road. Strength, and muscle building, is not a linear process.

Build muscle with the WH+ Build & Burn series

Ultimately, building and maintaining muscle mass is one of the strongest investments you can make in long-term health—especially as you age.

And lifting heavy is one effective way to provide muscle-building stimulus to the body—but it isn’t accessible, comfortable, or safe for everyone all the time. The goal is progressive challenge, and lighter loads can deliver that when you train with intention and effort.

“You do not need to lift heavy to build muscle, but you do need to train with intention,” Reiner says. “The best approach is the one that someone can perform consistently, safely, and with enough effort to challenge the muscle over time.”

Cori Ritchey, C.S.C.S., is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and condition coach and group fitness instructor. She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

#5011. Bitcoin Falls Further as Inflation, Trump Tariffs and AI Selloff Rattle Markets

Bitcoin Falls Further as Inflation, Trump Tariffs and AI Selloff Rattle Markets

Bitcoin fell below $58,000 Wednesday morning as stronger-than-expected U.S. economic growth, rising inflation and a fresh round of proposed tariffs from President Donald Trump's administration gave investors more reasons to sell.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.3%, the S&P 500 lost 3%, and Nvidia shed 8.7% as of 9:50 a.m. ET. Bitcoin hit a session low of $57,500 as the selloff on Wall Street spilled over into the crypto market.

Paradoxically, part of the problem is that the U.S. economy is doing better than expected. The Bureau of Economic Analysis revised its estimate of third-quarter GDP growth from 3.4% to 4.3% at an annualized rate, nearly double the 2.2% recorded in the second quarter.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

But the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, rose 3.8% year-over-year in October, up from 3.6% in September and matching a three-year high set in May. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 3.3%, compared with economists' expectations of 3.2% and September's reading of 3.1%.

“America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told AFP. Consumer spending increased in dollar terms in October but was flat after adjusting for inflation.

A growing economy gives the Fed more room to raise borrowing costs to bring inflation back toward its 2% target. After Wednesday's inflation release, traders were pricing in a 98% probability of a quarter-point increase in December, according to CME FedWatch data. Today odds are set at 94%.

The Fed held rates at between 3.75% and 4% in October after raising them in September for the first time in three years. Traders are also betting on further tightening in 2027, with another increase expected as early as January.

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative proposed tariffs targeting 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea, following investigations into government policies that encourage manufacturing production beyond market demand.

The proposed rates vary by country and product, with duties of up to 20% on some Chinese imports and up to 35% on Vietnamese goods, subject to adjustments and exemptions. For the EU, the proposed 15% rate accounts for certain existing duties rather than simply adding 15 percentage points to them.

The tariffs have not taken effect, and public hearings are scheduled to begin January 25. If importers pass the additional costs on to consumers, the duties could make the Fed's job of bringing inflation down even harder.

Meanwhile, Wall Street's enthusiasm over Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia didn't last very long. The chipmaker closed Monday up 31.5% but lost more than 6% Tuesday, while Anthropic closed at $81.91, below its $83 initial public offering price less than a week after its Nasdaq debut.

Higher interest rates make it more expensive to finance data centers and reduce the present value of future earnings. Both are particularly relevant for AI companies spending heavily today in anticipation of profits years down the road.

The selloff began well before Wall Street opened. South Korea's Kospi closed 6.16% lower, while spot gold fell 2% to $3,483.59 an ounce by 9:15 a.m. ET, according to Reuters.

Crypto investors were already in bad shape before Wednesday's economic data came out. Blockchain analytics firm Glassnode reported Tuesday that Bitcoin investors were realizing their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX and the subsequent market crash in November 2022, relative to the money that flowed into the asset over the preceding year.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have also recorded $4.94 billion in net outflows this November through Tuesday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, already making it their worst month since launching in January 2024.

The Fed's next interest rate decision is scheduled for December 9.

#5007. Galaxy Withdraws Call That Bitcoin’s Bear Market Ended in June

Galaxy has withdrawn its October call that bitcoin’s bear market ended in June, saying the technical signal behind it failed after seven straight weeks of losses and that the bear market is “very likely not over.”

Alex Thorn, Galaxy’s head of firmwide research, laid out the reversal in a report published Wednesday and sent to clients a day earlier. “We withdraw our call that the bear market ended in June,” the report said. “The signal it rested on has failed.”

The firm’s Oct. 26 note had argued that bitcoin had entered an accumulation phase. Galaxy said at the time that a weekly close back below the 50-week moving average that was not regained within a month would invalidate its technical case.

That is what happened. Bitcoin closed the week ended Nov. 8 at $74,968, 0.7% below the 50-week average, after seven weekly closes above it. It then closed the week ended Nov. 15 below the 200-week average, which Galaxy has described as the floor of past bear markets.

The week ended Nov. 22 closed at $61,104, 17.9% below the 50-week average and 10.4% below the 200-week average of $68,159. Bitcoin traded below its July 1 intraday low on Nov. 20 and reached $55,100 on Nov. 21, but the June 30 closing low of $58,525 held on a daily basis through Nov. 22.

Galaxy now treats that level as the line to watch. A daily close below $58,525 would be “the start of a move to a materially lower low,” the report said, and the firm would not treat such a close as a buying signal by itself.

History is not kind to breaks like that. In the seven prior bear market cases where bitcoin closed below a low that had stood for at least 60 days, the eventual low was at least 17% lower, with a median of 52%. Applied to the June low, that works out to about $48,500 and $28,200.

Bitcoin briefly slumped below $57,500 on Wednesday morning as the Nasdaq sank, but it ended the day back above $60,000 and has not posted a daily close below $58,525. It traded near $60,800 on Thursday morning.

Galaxy said two readings of the market disagree. By the calendar, this bear is old: Nov. 22 was day 412 since the Oct. 6, 2025, record, longer than the 163 to 406 days from high to low in the four prior bear markets.

By depth, it looks unfinished. Bitcoin’s 53% decline compares with drops of 77% to 93% in earlier bears. It also has not closed a day below its realized price of $53,205, something every prior bear did for at least 140 days, and only two of the 13 bottom signals Galaxy tracks have been met.

“The clock says this bear is overdue to end, the depth says it has further to fall, and we do not believe the price record alone can settle which,” the report said.

Flows have not helped. Galaxy estimates U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs hold about 1.24 million BTC, 9.7% below their October 2025 peak, after shedding 71,339 BTC, or $4.95 billion, since Oct. 4. November is shaping up as a record month for ETF outflows.

Galaxy said the other three parts of its October thesis, covering positioning, fundamentals and sentiment, are stronger now than when it published. Its proprietary Bitcoin Fear & Greed Index fell to 5.2 on Nov. 21, its lowest reading since June 30, 2022.

To swing back toward its October view, Galaxy wants a weekly close above the 200-week average and then the 50-week average, now $74,401, with the June weekly closing low of $59,517 holding. A weekly close below realized price would point to a deeper bear.

“We are not trying to call the low,” the report said. “Until one gives way, we will judge the market on weekly closes rather than headlines.”

#5005. Elon Musk’s X Wins Court Judgment Against Alleged Bitcoin Bot Farm Operators

Elon Musk’s X Wins Court Judgment Against Alleged Bitcoin Bot Farm Operators

Elon Musk’s X has won a default judgment in a UK court against two men accused of running a network of Bitcoin-focused accounts that gamed the platform’s creator-payout system, a case that prompted Musk to warn fraudsters: “Don’t mess with X.”

London’s High Court entered the judgment on Nov. 20 against Vivek Kumar Sen and Zamyang Sherpa after neither man filed an acknowledgment of service or a defence, with Master Teverson ruling in favor of X without a trial.

A default judgment means the court entered the order because the defendants failed to engage, not because the allegations were tested and proven. Either defendant can apply within seven days of being served to have the order varied or set aside.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The case dates to a claim issued Sept. 21, when X sued the pair and unidentified accomplices for allegedly operating a coordinated bot army to inflate engagement and siphon money from its Creator Revenue Sharing program.

According to the claim, six enrolled accounts, including handles such as @Vivek4real_ and @Bitcoin_Teddy, were amplified by three additional accounts using likes, reposts and replies to manufacture the engagement that drove payouts.

Crucially, the judgment awards no money yet. Because X sued for “an unspecified sum,” the order states the amount of damages and interest will be decided later at a separate Disposal Hearing.

X has estimated the improperly obtained revenue at no less than £207,384 (about $271,000) and said it is seeking at least £75,000 ($98,000) more in investigation and remediation costs. Those are the company’s claimed figures, not sums the court has granted.

X General Counsel James Burnham announced the ruling, writing that the company had “sued people who abused Creator Revenue Sharing by operating a network of accounts to manipulate engagement” and that the court had now entered judgment against two of them.

“We aren’t kidding around,” he added. “Fraudsters worldwide: Do not mess with X.” Musk reposted the statement with his own terse endorsement.

Even once damages are set, recovering the money is a separate matter that depends on whatever assets Sen and Sherpa hold.

The case reflects the broader strain of the “engagement economy,” where platforms paying creators based on activity have become targets for coordinated manipulation.

X retired Creator Revenue Sharing, which launched in 2023 and paid out based on engagement, on Sept. 7, replacing it the next day with Original Content Rewards, a system it says emphasizes original material over raw engagement volume, a shift partly aimed at the kind of gaming alleged here.

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

BIT Asset Management's BBIT fund debuted on SIX Swiss Exchange with 350 BTC in assets and a 0.19% annual expense ratio.

BIT Asset Management's spot bitcoin ETF has begun trading on the SIX Swiss Exchange, with the company saying it is the first ETF in Switzerland to hold bitcoin directly.

The fund trades under the ticker BBIT in U.S. dollars and Swiss francs. It debuted with 350 BTC (currently worth over $20 million) in assets and has a total expense ratio of 0.19% a year. BIT said BBIT is currently Europe's only spot bitcoin ETF.

The Jacobi FT Wilshire Bitcoin ETF was Europe's first spot bitcoin ETF when it debuted on Euronext Amsterdam in August 2023. Euronext has listed the fund as inactive since Feb. 2, 2026. Jacobi Asset Management (Holdings) Ltd appointed a liquidator on Feb. 26, 2026, as part of a creditors' voluntary liquidation, according to a notice in The Gazette.

BBIT is publicly offered only in Switzerland. BIT pointed to investors outside the U.S., including Asian investors who hold assets with Swiss private banks, as a potential audience. It did not specify which investors outside Switzerland could buy the fund.

"If investors want a US product, they have plenty of choice. If they want a non-US product in a neutral jurisdiction, until now they really didn't," said Cynthia Wu, co-founder and chief commercial officer of BIT. "BBIT gives investors outside the US a regulated, liquid way to hold Bitcoin through the bank or broker they already use, with the asset protection of a fund."

The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority, or FINMA, approved BBIT on Oct. 20 after an 18-month review, according to BIT Asset Management. FINMA exempted the fund from diversification rules, allowing it to invest entirely in bitcoin.

Most bitcoin products listed in Europe are structured as debt securities, BIT Asset Management said, noting that BBIT is a Swiss investment fund. The firm said Swiss-regulated AMINA Bank holds the fund's bitcoin assets separately from BIT Asset Management's own assets. BBIT also allows in-kind subscriptions, letting investors exchange bitcoin directly for ETF shares without first converting it to cash.

"The economic exposure of a fund and a note can look very similar when everything goes well. The difference is what happens when it doesn't," said Friedrich Herzog, chief investment officer of BIT Asset Management. "The segregation of duties and responsibilities of counterparties is by design, and it is why products like this take years to build and approve."

BIT Asset Management was previously known as Crypto Finance (Asset Management) AG. BIT said the group acquired the Swiss asset manager in 2024 and renamed it Matrixport Asset Management AG before it took its current name.

The BBIT listing comes as bitcoin has fallen back below $60,000. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs saw about $4.94 billion in net outflows in November through Tuesday, according to SoSoValue data. The U.S. ETFs began trading in January 2024.

#5002. The Secrets to Whole-Life Training

A well-rounded fitness routine that will enhance all of your activities and adventures starts with your feet.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There’s more to getting fit than chasing a PR or sweating through another bootcamp class. The real payoff? Being ready for the next workout, the weekend adventure, the everyday hustle, and all the years ahead.

The key is making different types of exercise work together, rather than relying on any one activity. This multifaceted and well-rounded approach to training means you’re working more than the muscles, because you’re focused on the movements.

When you approach training this way, you’re literally starting from the ground up. “Every single step you take, your foot is the first thing that hits the ground,” says Jen Perez, DC, a chiropractic physician who combines clinical practice and education to help people improve foot health and lower-body function. “It’s the first thing that interfaces with the world around you, what has to be strong and springy when you want to run or jump or dance or ski.”

A whole-life, well-rounded training plan comes down to five essentials, according to Courtney Conley, DC, a best-selling author and chiropractic physician with more than two decades of clinical experience:

Cardio and strength may already be part of your routine, but the others can be easier to overlook; especially because they deliver numerous movement benefits that you may not equate them with. For example, Conley emphasizes that power training isn’t just for athletes; it also has practical life applications. “Getting up and out of your chair, having good reaction time, and making sure you don’t fall if you step off a curb and trip are all part of that category,” she says.

Mobility means moving freely through a full range of motion, while balance helps you adjust to changing surfaces and react when your footing shifts—it isn’t just holding a tree pose. “There are thousands of nerve endings in each foot that help communicate to our brain where we are in space,” Perez explains. That feedback, combined with the feet’s ability to grip the ground, helps keep you steady.

Recovery is what allows your body to benefit from hard training, yet Conley says it’s often ignored: “I think one of the biggest mistakes is that people don’t recover.” Sleep, adequate nutrition, and lighter days that deliberately scale back workout volume or intensity give your body time to adapt and help you come back ready for your next workout.

The work you do in the gym should go beyond just trying to look good and prepare you for the demands of everyday movement. For strength and power work, Conley recommends deadlifts and kettlebell swings to train the hip-hinge pattern, along with farmer’s carries to build strength in the core and lower body. “I love all that functional movement,” she says. “A sled push is also great, because as your heel comes off the ground, you’re hitting all the intrinsic muscles of your foot.”

Certain machine exercises may not seem so functional but can address specific weaknesses. For instance, Conley says she often uses seated calf raises to strengthen the tissues around the Achilles and leg extensions to isolate the quadriceps. She also recommends plyometrics—quick, explosive jumping and hopping drills—to develop power. “Try double-leg and single-leg hops, forward and backward, side to side, and zigzag moves,” she says, recommending five or six sets of 10 reps per exercise for plyometric movements.

Ankle and big-toe mobility are number one on Conley’s priority list for things you should focus on outside of your regular workouts. “When you can’t propel through the ankle, you’re going to get there by extending the knee so you can push yourself forward,” she says. “People come in with knee or back pain when oftentimes it’s an ankle problem.” She suggests making mobility a regular part of the week rather than waiting until something feels stiff or restricted. Even a short dedicated session can help you maintain the range of motion your training requires.

Perez says your feet also adapt to the surface beneath you and absorb force. “If you think of your foot like a trampoline, every single step we take, whether walking or running, the foot needs to be able to lower, which is that mobility piece, then it needs to be able to spring back up.”

Perez recommends two simple drills to improve foot mobility and strength: the Foot Handshake, where you weave the fingers of one hand between the toes of the opposite foot and gently circle the foot at the ankle; and Lift, Spread, and Reach, where you lift all five toes, spread them apart, then reach them forward as you lower them.

Another way you can activate your feet during training is to choose your shoes wisely. When it comes to footwear, Perez has one non-negotiable regardless of the activity: a wide toe box that lets your toes spread naturally. “If your toes are more narrow than the ball of your foot, that tells me we’ve got some work to do,” she says. In practice, that can mean adding foot mobility and strength drills to your routine and choosing shoes that let your toes spread naturally.

Perez favors Altra Fit, both for her own footwear and when recommending shoes to others, because it gives the forefoot more room than a traditionally tapered toe box. Conley’s experience shows how the amount of cushioning that feels right can change over time as your foot gets stronger and needs more targeted footwear. She started out in the Altra FWD VIA 2, a cushioned shoe with the original (read: roomiest) FootShape™ and a 4 mm drop that felt familiar coming from conventional running shoes. “I was getting some toe splay and my foot was getting stronger,” she recalls. “Now I put them on, and it’s too much shoe for me because I don’t need as much cushioning.”

That’s where having options comes in. Altra’s Torin 9 offers a more moderate level of cushioning, standard footshape (secure midfoot), and a zero-drop platform that is good for running and still takes advantage of the Altra Fit that helps your feet get stronger as you log miles. For a lower-profile option, the Altra Escalante 5 has low cushioning, a 24 mm stack height, zero drop, and the original, roomiest FootShape fit.

“You’ll want to use the least amount of shoe assistance necessary for the activity,” Perez recommends. A lower-profile, more flexible shoe, like the Escalante 5, offers more ground feel for strength training, while extra cushioning or rocker geometry, found in the Torin 9 and FWD VIA 2, may be useful on longer runs. Conley agrees that a plush running shoe isn’t necessarily the best tool for lifting. “You can’t feel the ground,” she says of maximalist shoes. “You’re standing on something that decreases your sensory acuity.”

If multidimensional fitness is new to you, Conley recommends starting with manageable strength work (two or three days a week), walking, and one or two mobility or foot exercises, and build gradually as your strength and capacity improve. “Do things that challenge you, but not to the point where you start to feel overwhelmed,” she says.

If you already work out or run regularly, consider what’s missing from your routine while prioritizing your main goal. Conley suggests making room for mobility, balance, and power work, and fitting short foot-strength and mobility exercises into existing workouts. Do it while you’re fresh, adjusting your workload when running volume increases or recovery suffers.

The goal isn’t to do everything all the time or become an expert at every type of training. It’s to build a body that can keep doing the things you love. Run the trails. Lift the heavy stuff. Hike the mountain. Get down on the floor with your kids and grandkids—and have the strength and mobility to get back up again.

#5001. Bitcoin Price Trades Near $61,300 as Tech Stock Futures Rally

The bitcoin price traded near $61,300 on Friday morning, as tech stock futures jumped ahead of a holiday-shortened session on Wall Street. Bitcoin price is on track for its first weekly gain after seven straight weekly losses, though it is still down about 20% in November.

The bitcoin price was up about 1.7% early Friday and set to add 4.8% for the week, Investing.com reported, extending a recovery from a two-year low of $57,325.70 hit earlier in the week. Bitcoin slumped below $57,500 on Wednesday as the Nasdaq sank at the open, before a late rebound in tech shares lifted risk assets.

Short sellers helped fuel the bounce. Shorts made up 77% of $84.7 million in bitcoin liquidations over the past day, while futures open interest was little changed. That suggests forced short covering, rather than fresh leverage, supplied much of the lift.

Nasdaq 100 futures rose 2.2% by 6:42 a.m. ET, Reuters reported, as investors returned from Thanksgiving and piled back into battered AI-linked shares. Nvidia gained 3.6% in premarket trading, while AMD climbed 4.4% and Broadcom added 3.4%. S&P 500 futures rose 1.6%, and Dow futures gained 1.3%.

“There have been some signs that the tech selloff has stabilised for now, and that risk appetite is returning to markets,” Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note cited by Reuters. The S&P 500 is headed for its best week since April, though it remains on course for its worst November since 2008.

Bitcoin price has followed that rebound but lagged it. The major U.S. stock indexes are each up around 4% on the week, and silver jumped about 7% to above $44 an ounce on Friday while gold added 2.5% to above $3,670. Stocks close early at 1 p.m. ET, and the bond market shuts at 2 p.m.

The macro backdrop still weighs on the bitcoin price. Traders are almost fully pricing in a Federal Reserve rate hike in December after data this week showed the economy grew faster than first estimated in the third quarter and inflation accelerated in October, Reuters reported. Third-quarter GDP growth was revised up to 4.3%, and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.84%.

Spot bitcoin ETFs are also still losing cash. The U.S. funds lost $453 million on Wednesday, their seventh straight day of outflows, with BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounting for $329.7 million. That pushed November outflows to about $5.39 billion, extending what was already a record month for the funds.

Crypto stocks face their own test in Friday’s short session. Strategy shares rose 3.1% to $79.96 on Wednesday, while Coinbase gained 1.3% to $103.72. Bitcoin miners that have moved into AI hosting tracked the tech rally, with IREN and Cipher Digital each gaining 8% in premarket trading.

Mining economics remain tight with the bitcoin price this low. CleanSpark has weighed selling more bitcoin than it mines after a $987 million loss, and network mining difficulty jumped 7.61% early Friday, reversing most of a 9.13% drop on Nov. 14. That means miners must spend more computing power for each bitcoin they earn.

In options markets, about $7 billion of bitcoin contracts expired at 3 a.m. ET Friday, with traders positioned defensively going into the expiry. Over the past day, four of the six busiest bitcoin options were calls, three of them at $62,000 to $64,000 strikes, though the single busiest contract was a Dec. 25 put at $50,000.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,300.

US spot bitcoin ETFs have recorded $5.39 billion in cumulative net outflows so far this month, already surpassing the previous monthly record with several days remaining.

U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds are on track for their worst month on record, with cumulative net outflows reaching roughly $5.39 billion in November amid heightened bitcoin volatility.

On Wednesday, Spot bitcoin ETFs posted $453.1 million in net outflows, extending their negative flow streak to seven days, according to SoSoValue data. BlackRock's IBIT led the outflows with $329.7 million, followed by funds from Grayscale and Bitwise.

Notably, with several trading days left in November, the month's cumulative net outflows have already surpassed those of any previous month.

Spot Ethereum ETFs also recorded $68.5 million in net outflows on Wednesday, marking their ninth consecutive day of negative flows. Their cumulative net outflows amounted to $1.3 billion so far this month, compared with $1.6 billion in October.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) rose 2.6% over the past 24 hours to $60,525 as of 2:30 a.m. ET Thursday, after falling to as low as around $57,300 the day before, according to The Block's BTC price page. Ethereum Ethereum (ETH) gained 2.3% to trade at $1,690, BNB climbed 2.4%, and XRP added 3.8%.

"Persistent ETF outflows weaken spot demand, increasing downside risks and limiting sustainable rallies," said Dominick John, analyst at Zeus Research.

Dan Khus, chief analyst at LVRG Research, told The Block that the outflow streak signals sustained institutional de-risking that continues to pressure prices and force traders to prioritize capital preservation over aggressive positioning until flows stabilize.

Justin d'Anethan, head of research at Arctic Digital, said the recent crypto volatility is mainly driven by macro factors, "as one can see all risk assets retracing aggressively."

"Blame it on the Democratic win, or rate expectations, or geopolitical conflict, or an AI trade recalibration, but every investor out there is evaluating how much risk they've taken and should hold moving forward," said d'Anethan.

Galaxy Head of Firmwide Research Alex Thorn has withdrawn the firm's October call that bitcoin's bear market ended in June. Thorn said the team now treats a daily close below $58,525 — the June 30 closing low — as the start of a move toward a materially lower low.

Similarly, 21Shares said Tuesday that it expects rallies to fade until stablecoin supply and ETF inflows recover. The firm sees the realized price near $53,250 as one of the low levels to watch.

Rick Maeda, head of markets at Laevitas, said Galaxy's bearish pivot is "understandable" as the near-term recovery catalysts and bullish signals have been limited for bitcoin and the broader crypto asset class. Maeda noted that the macro backdrop and fear of AI progress have continued to weigh on crypto assets, "not to mention tax-loss harvesting as we head into the year-end period."

While signs of a near-term recovery remain limited, LVRG's Khus pointed to several potential catalysts for a rebound. "Catalysts such as clearer Fed policy signals, cooling inflation data, or a decisive shift back to net inflows could quickly restore institutional demand and support a rebound," he said.
