#4996. 9 Best Cooling Sheets for More Comfortable Sleep, Tested by Editors

We tested dozens of cooling sheets. My Sheets Rock makes the best.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I always thought cooling sheets were a marketing gimmick until I actually tried them while I was nine months pregnant—in the middle of July. It was the first time in months that I didn’t wake up with my sweaty hair matted against my head, and I’ve never looked back.

It’s important to get this out of the way now: Cooling sheets aren’t magic. They’re not going to keep you from sweating if you sleep under a heavy comforter or it’s warm in your bedroom at night. But they do cause a noticeable difference in how you feel between the sheets, and are one more element to help regulate your body temperature at night.

These are a few of our favorite sheet sets, but read on for more detailed reviews:

“The ideal temperature for sleeping is no cooler than 66 degrees and no warmer than 72 degrees,” says neuroscientist and sleep specialist Allison Brager, PhD. “This was study-approved, tested, and evaluated by some NASA scientists.” Resting in this temperate climate can support better sleep and, ultimately, improved health. Regularly shortchanging your sleep leads to a higher risk of obesity, depression, and type 2 diabetes, along with other health issues. But having good, consistent sleep can do the opposite.

That’s why, even though cooling sheets are usually more expensive than regular sheets, they’re a worthwhile investment that will help support more restorative sleep, Brager says, and, as a result, improve your overall quality of life.

So, how can you tell which bedding option will help you hit that not-so-hot spot? Cooling sheets—especially those made from fabrics like microfiber, linen, and bamboo—can help keep your body at the right temp for restful sleep. The best cooling sheets can help reduce heat buildup and manage moisture, but your comfort also depends on your room and bedding.

The Regulator sheets are made from rayon derived from bamboo and felt lightweight, silky, and cool to the touch, according to our testers.

“They’re very soft, and I’m able to wake up not sweaty,” says Women’s Health digital designer Taryn Colbert, who has zero complaints about these sheets.

WH contributor and self-professed "hot sleeper" Lily Wohlner is also a fan. She had never owned a set of cooling sheets, but quickly fell in love with these. They're "super thin, which automatically makes them nice and light,” Wohlner says. “But they're also temperature-regulating and moisture-wicking, so you stay fresh and cool while you snooze.” She also loves how silky smooth they feel against the skin without that "crunchy" feeling found in lesser, lower-quality sheets.

There is one catch to the ultra-lightweight design, however. "Due to their weight, I find that these sheets tend to bunch up at the bottom of my bed, which I don't love," Wohlner says. "Every time I go to make my bed, I have to fish under my comforter to find them, which adds time to the already dreaded process." (Colbert hasn’t experienced this.)

It's not a deal-breaker for us, but something to be aware of. Plus, we found that the natural stretch of these sheets means making (or re-making) the bed is a snap.

Bamboo is often touted as more eco-friendly because it's possible to harvest more per acre than cotton and is typically grown without pesticides. However, the experts we spoke with warned that the raw material goes through serious chemical refinement before it's turned into bedding.

Overall, our team loved these sheets for their buttery soft, featherweight design and the ability to keep us cool and sweat-free even on the hottest summer nights. They're a great midrange set that we recommend for anyone looking to level up from the cheapest available options (like Mellanni's four-piece Iconic Sheet Set), but who isn't quite ready to splurge on an ultra-luxe set.

“Jill of all trades; master of none.” That's the perfect way to describe Mellanni's Iconic Collection, including the four-piece set of cooling sheets we tested for this year's roundup. These sheets aren't the softest, the most luxurious, or the absolute best at cooling. But they are a solid all-around buy that feels better, looks better, and cools better than most other sets that cost three times as much.

"My girlfriend and I have slept on these for the last month, and we've been pleasantly surprised by how good they feel for the price," Richard says. "They feel much better and cozier against the skin than most other sheets I've tested in this price range."

Fellow tester and self-described hot sleeper Janie Booth, associate video producer at WH, also praises the feel of these sheets. “They are very soft,” she says.

The synthetic microfiber construction in this sheet set isn't purposely designed for cooling. In fact, the weave is tighter than other sheets made with natural fibers. But the material is thin enough to be surprisingly breathable, without feeling threadbare. "I actually took these glamping on a long, hot, late June weekend," Richard says. "For sticky, sweaty nights, the thickness of these sheets was perfect, and I found them much more breathable than most microfiber sheets."

On the downside, that same microfiber—polyester, really—construction means these aren't as absorbent or moisture-wicking as natural alternatives either. So, they're not as good at whisking away sweat to help further cool your body.

Like most microfiber fabrics, these sheets are surprisingly durable, though, thanks to the previously mentioned tight weave. We've found they hold up well, even after repeated washings with no loose threads, shedding, or fading. (Booth noticed some pilling, but Richard didn’t.) Plus, they're more wrinkle-resistant than most.

The biggest thing these cooling sheets have going for them is price. They're significantly cheaper (in some cases, by more than 75 percent) than every other set in this year's roundup. Plus, with Amazon's generous free shipping and free returns policy, it's almost like you're getting a legit in-home sleep trial.

One additional bonus is that these sheets are available in a much wider selection of colors and patterns than any other we tested. That's especially nice if you're keen to match the look of your new cooling sheets to the rest of your bedroom decor.

There are a lot of high-tech fabric blends out there designed to keep you cool, but classic cotton sheets can still work wonders. Brooklinen’s Classic Percale Core Sheet Set is a favorite in my household—so much so that I’ll try to wash them quickly when I do laundry to get them back on my mattress before I need to swap in a different set. These were the sheets I splurged on when I was heavily pregnant and hot. They still feel luxurious and crisp, even though I’ve had them in heavy rotation for two years.

The sheets are made with percale cotton, which means it’s woven into a grid pattern to give it a crisp, cool feel. It’s almost like a dress shirt, but softer, and with a noticeable coolness when you slide between the sheets.

Christian Gollayan, style and reviews director at Men's Health and Women's Health, is also a fan. “I’m a hot sleeper and usually need my bedroom below 69 degrees to avoid getting sweaty,” he says. “These kept me comfortable through fall, winter, and spring.”

Gollayan says his sheets held up “remarkably well” for nearly two years with weekly washings. When he did sweat in deep summer, Gollayan says his sheets didn’t hold onto an odor the way some other sets he’s tried have. The sheets have thoughtful details that I love, too, like envelope closures to keep your pillows from sliding out and tags that designate which end of the fitted sheet is the long and short side.

While Gollayan and I both enjoy these sheets, he noticed some fraying in his set after two years. (I haven’t had the same experience, although the rich blue color in my tandem stripes is fading.) They also felt a little stiff at first, but quickly soften up with time and repeat washings. They’re not the cheapest cooling sheets you’ll find, but they’re pretty durable and luxe.

Casper is perhaps best known for its excellent cooling mattresses. But you might be surprised to learn the company also makes great cooling bedding. After testing over a dozen cooling sheets, Casper's Hyperlite Sheet Set earned our 'Best Runner-Up' spot for its soft, ultra-lightweight feel, the fact it looks more premium than its price should allow, and, most importantly, its 100 percent Tencel Lyocell construction. The fabric excels at fighting sweat and overheating, thanks to its structure, which absorbs and releases moisture while promoting good airflow.

“They're definitely cooling without being too ‘cold,’” says WH digital designer and tester Leeann Mattern. Fellow tester Mike Richard also praises the sheets’ lightweight, cooling feel, which he says is great year-round. But, in warmer weather, he says they do an excellent job at regulating temperature and wicking away sweat and moisture. That's thanks in large part to the tencel lyocell material and the unique, vented grid-weave pattern that Casper uses to help promote better airflow while you sleep. Bonus: Our team loved that same grid pattern elevates the vibe of these sheets above the traditional (and often boring) flat aesthetic of most sheets with a lightly textured look and feel.

We're hard-pressed to find much to complain about with these cooling sheets, but there are a few minor concerns to keep in mind. "My only gripe is that I wish they were a little softer because they're not quite as buttery or luxurious as the true bamboo and bamboo blend options we tested," Richard says. That's largely due to their lower 200-thread-count construction (incidentally, that was the lowest of any sheets we tested this year). "I did find that they soften after a few washes, however, and hold up well to repeated machine-washings, too."

Mattern also says the lightweight fabric allows patterns in her mattress and pillow to show through, so that’s something to be aware of if you’re especially concerned about aesthetics. On that note, our team of sleep testers were a bit bummed by the lack of available color options—this sheet set only comes in white.

We would also love it if Casper expanded its return policy beyond the lackluster 30 days. That's surprisingly thin compared to the competition, and the sheets must be returned in their original, unused condition, which doesn't allow for a true "sleep trial."

Of course, you don't have to spend hundreds to score a decent set of cooling sheets. But, sometimes, you really do get what you pay for. That's true of Bedgear's Ver-Tex Sheet Set. They're pricier than most we tested this year, but oh so worth it with a performance-minded design that keeps you cool and stays put, even during your most "vigorous" bed activities.

The Ver-Tex Sheet Set is the only one in this year's roundup made of 100 percent nylon. Like many synthetic materials, nylon isn't typically absorbent or very good at wicking away moisture. "I initially planned to test these out in my guest room," Richard says. "But my girlfriend and I loved how cool-to-the-touch they were, and found them way softer and airier than we expected, so we wound up putting them on our bed."

The nylon is extremely breathable, allowing them to cool better than most. In very humid environments (think Miami in August), however, we did notice that they felt slightly clammier than other natural fabric sets our team tested. “This is such a ridiculous thing to say, but they almost did their job too well,” says fellow tester and WH social media editor Alyssa Cruz. “I sometimes wake up cold and need to add extra blankets.” Because of this, she plans to switch them out during the chillier winter months.

Still, our team agrees that these sheets are worth the $300 price tag. “I love the feeling the most,” Cruz says. “These are the softest sheets I have ever felt, and almost feel like activewear. They make falling asleep feel luxurious.”

Plus, one of this set's biggest selling points is its ability to stretch and provide an extremely good fit, thanks to Bedgear's unique Powerband. It's a thick, full-band elastic designed to grip the bottom of your mattress so it won't slip. The pillowcases included with the Ver-Tex sets also feature this same band, so we never wound up with our pillows inching their way out of the case. Everything stays put, so you're not left remaking the bed every night before tucking in.

There's almost nothing we dislike about these best-in-class cooling sheets. But we do wish they were available in more than four colors. They're also not sold in smaller sizes like Twin, Twin XL, or Full, which may or may not be a deal-breaker for you.

Lastly, these are among the priciest cooling sheets we tested over the past year. Still, we think you get what you pay for with this set. They're extremely durable, cool better than almost every other set we tested, and the ultra-snug fit for both the sheets and pillowcases is second to none.

PeachSkinSheets’ Classic Collection has a brushed polyester fabric that our testers found super soft. Somehow PeachSkinSheets manages to thread that needle (pun intended) with its Classic Collection. With an airy, breathable, smart poly-fiber construction, these sheets are surprisingly effective at keeping you cool, calm, and collected.

"I tested these in our guest suite, and the in-laws (self-described 'fussy' sleepers) and I both agreed that these do an incredible job at keeping you cool during the night," Richard says. "They feel more premium, more luxurious than the price tag would suggest." But more importantly, our entire test staff found these kept us cool while also doing a reasonable job of managing sweat and moisture. The athletic-grade construction is lighter than traditional cotton, and they breathe more like high-end (think Lululemon) athleisure apparel.

The sheets are OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 certified, meaning they have been tested against limits for harmful substances. "My girlfriend has extremely sensitive skin, and even basic synthetics like polyester don't always agree with her, sometimes causing rashes and irritation," Richard says. "We were initially skeptical about these poly-fiber sheets, but she's had zero issues and finds them extremely comfortable."

The feel of these sheets was also a perk for WH associate style and reviews editor Shannen Zitz. “The sheets are super soft and smooth without causing me to overheat at night,” she says.

Zitz praises the deep corners of the fitted sheet, too. “I love that the fitted sheet actually stays on my bed,” she says. “My biggest issue with sheets is when they slip off the corners after just a few nights, but these have really deep corners so they stay put really well.” Every set also includes an extender panel, allowing the sheets to fit extra-deep (up to 22-inch) mattresses which covers just about every model on the market.

Unlike most of the competition, they're available in more than 30 colorways—everything from basic white and navy to bolder options like gold and neon orange—making it easy to match the aesthetic of your current bedroom setup.

After several months of testing, we found the Classic Collection cooling sheets to be extremely durable. "Even after repeated machine-washing and with two cats in my house, these sheets have stood up to teeth, claws, pills, pulls, and fading," Richard says. "Plus, fresh out of the wash, the wrinkles release almost instantly after making the bed, so I never have to worry about ironing them." The only gripe, per Zitz, is that the top sheet felt a little short. “I toss and turn a lot and, after a night or two, I find the bottom of the sheet comes untucked pretty easily,” she says. “If you like your sheets to feel really snug, it requires re-tucking.”

PeachSkinSheets also shines with a solid, 30-day return policy. Like SlumberCloud, it's more like an in-home sleep trial. Even opened bedding can be returned within 30 days for a full refund, so it's truly risk-free to try them out at home.

Most cooling bedding products are designed to draw away and evaporate moisture. But that means they only start working after you're already sweating and are probably miserable. Slumber Cloud's Performance Sheets take a different tack with a uniquely blended construction that actively regulates temperature the entire time you're sleeping to (ideally) keep you cool and comfortable before sweat ever becomes an issue.

The secret sauce to Slumber Cloud's Performance Sheets is a blend of reactive Tencel with Outlast viscose. Tencel is already one of our favorite fibers for cooling sheets, but the addition of Outlast levels up the entire setup. "I've used Outlast-infused hiking apparel before, and it's incredibly effective at regulating body temperature in hot or cold environments," Richard says. "The addition of Outlast in these sheets delivers best-in-class moisture-wicking, which is a game-changer if you're a hot (and potentially clammy) sleeper." The 300-thread-count material might appear to be lower quality than higher-end 500-plus-thread-count alternatives. But, these feel every bit softer than many premium sheets we've previously tested.

These sheets are soft to the touch, according to fellow tester and WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson. “But my absolute favorite thing about these sheets, which I've never encountered with another set, is the additional elastic band at the corners of the fitted sheet that help it wrap around virtually any size mattress you can imagine,” she says. Compared to the traditional "corner-sewn" elastics found in most traditional fitted sheets, the bands in this sheet set help keep it firmly in place.

One especially nice feature of all of Slumber Cloud's bedding: it offers a 30-night trial for purchases made directly from the brand.

If you’re an extra-hot sleeper, however, you may want to look elsewhere. While Wilkinson found these sheets cooling, she says that, despite claims about being designed with “NASA cooling technology,” they didn’t seem to cool her off better than her previous sheet set. Still, they are great at wicking moisture and are incredibly durable.

(Pro tip: The Performance Sheet Set is, in our opinion, Slumber Cloud's best cooling sheet set. But, if you're looking for almost-as-good performance with a classic sheet feel, opt for its Essential Sheet Set which blends cotton with Outlast fibers.)

If you love the silky smoothness of cotton sateen sheets, Sijo’s AiryWeight Eucalyptus Sheets offer a similar feel while being 70 percent more moisture-absorbing. Made with naturally hypoallergenic Tencel Lyocell, the glossy silk-like texture of the sheets is a great option for those with sensitive skin, especially if certain materials make you feel itchy. Plus, the set boasts OEKO-TEX and Asthma and Allergy Friendly certifications.

“The feel of these are incredible,” says WH fitness editor Cori Ritchey. “With cooling sheets, I tend to fear they're going to be too slick and not cozy. These are kind of the perfect blend.” The sheets feel silky but not slippery, she adds.

At $185 for a queen-size set, these Sijo sheets aren’t cheap, but they are long lasting. The brand claims the sheets survived 2,000 rubs without pilling in lab testing. They passed Ritchey’s personal durability test, too: “They wash very nicely—they don't seem to lose their texture the longer you use them,” she says. And for those of us whose top sheet ends up on the floor most nights, you can subtract the flat sheet from the set for a $75 discount.

One of the downsides of the sheets is the two-month return window that only applies if the bedding is unopened—but there is a catch here. Sijo offers a 30-night bedding trial for eligible direct purchases. Return-shipping charges depend on whether you purchased Checkout+, so check the terms before ordering. Some customers have also noted that the sheets shrink a little after the first wash (we didn’t notice this during testing, but it’s worth flagging).

Some hot sleepers merely need sheets that are breathable throughout the night, while others prefer bedding that is immediately cool to the touch. If you want a set of sheets that feels like sleeping on the cool side of the pillow all night long, Sijo’s AiryWeight Eucalyptus Sheets are for you. “I'm normally a hot sleeper and these have kept me cool and comfortable,” Ritchey says.

Linen sheets are a great option for hot sleepers, if you’re willing to spend a little more. Brooklinen’s Linen Core Sheets are made with 100 percent European flax that softens with each wash, although they may be a little rough for sensitive skin right out of the box. The sheets are breathable yet they have a weight to them, which makes them great for year-round use.

“These sheets are so soft and cozy—truly the most comfortable material I have ever slept on,” says WH associate editor Olivia Luppino. “I actively look forward to getting into bed with them.” She describes the sheets as plush to the touch, while still maintaining a sleekness that gives them a cooling feel. “They definitely keep me cool in warm summer months,” she says. “I’m very into these sheets.”

That said, one of the (few) downsides is the $300-plus price tag, which is expensive but not outrageous when it comes to linen sheets. Plus, Brooklinen tends to run frequent sales, so it’s not unusual to see a 25 percent discount. The sheets have gotten softer with each wash, but at the same time they wear like iron with no snagging, pulling, or pilling to be found.

They are also OEKO-TEX certified and come with the longest return window of our favorite cooling sheets at a whopping 365 days. If you’re looking to make an investment that will last and keep you cool in any climate, Brooklinen’s Linen Core Sheets are worth the splurge.

To curate a list of the best cooling sheets, we recruited eight Women's Health staffers to personally vet a wide range of sets in various temperatures and environments over the past year. For instance, we slept in Casper's Hyperlite Sheet Set in July with no air-conditioning, glamped with Mellanni's Iconic Collection in New Hampshire, and cozied up in SlumberCloud's Performance Sheet Set with the window open in 80-degree heat “for science.” Then, our testing editors narrowed the selections by evaluating each sheet set based on style, fit, price point, comfort, breathability, moisture management, softness, durability after washing, wrinkling or pilling, and value.

It probably goes without saying that sheet material matters above all else. Natural fibers, like linen and cotton, are often best, according to Brager. They tend to be more breathable and absorbent (more on why that's actually a good thing below) than others, which means they won't trap heat that can make you sweat as you catch your Z's.

Your sheets’ weave is the pattern used to hold the threads together to make the fabric. Percale is generally considered the best weave for hot sleepers. This type of weave uses a simple pattern that maximizes airflow and has a lightweight feel, lowering the odds it will trap body heat while you snooze.

It’s generally recommended that you avoid sateen or flannel sheets if you’re looking for a cooling feel. These tend to be denser and hold onto heat as a result.

There are so many factors that go into how cool you feel when you slip between the sheets at night, including the temperature of your room, your body temperature, the weight of your comforter, and your mattress composition. But we sweat a lot throughout the night. "If you don't have something that's absorbent, you will marinate in sweat," Young says. That's why natural materials that are highly absorbent, like linen and cotton, are important. "Even more important than that is wicking, which means getting moisture to the surface for evaporation," says Young. The two of these features working in tandem is what keeps you both dry and cool.

Moisture-wicking sheets can be one element to help keep you cool at night. These sheets are specially designed to pull moisture away from your skin and evaporate, allowing you to feel cooler, faster. They also tend to feel a little airier than other sheets.

That doesn’t mean you won’t ever feel hot if you use moisture-wicking sheets—again, there’s a lot happening when you sleep that can influence your body’s temperature. But you can usually feel a difference between how you feel when using moisture-wicking sheets and other types of sheets.

Beyond the material of your cooling sheets, the quality of that material is important. Back in the day, thread count was the single most important measure of quality in bedding. Anything above 600-thread-count was often considered good, while 800 and above was downright luxurious. But advances in technology have allowed us to create sheets with a 1,500, even 2,000, thread count. That’s not necessarily a good thing, as that figure can be inflated and used as a marketing gimmick.

Plus, super-high thread-count sheets usually aren’t all they're cracked up to be. “My experience with those is that they’re not strong, and they don’t hold up well,” says Deborah Young, owner of TheTextileExpert.com and a clinical assistant professor of textiles at Arizona State University. “They are seductively soft, but for me, there’s a point of diminishing returns.”

Thread count can be a measure of quality, but you'll want to consider other factors, too, especially when shopping for the best cooling sheets. Some manufacturers rely on GSM (or grams per square meter) as this is a measure of weight rather than thread density.

Young's most important tip for hot sleepers, however, is that they may actually benefit from sheets with a lower thread count (like 400). A higher thread count often means the sheets are denser, offering better coverage, but a hot sleeper would probably want to avoid this.

It depends. Every brand we recommend below offers a return policy with a minimum 30-day term. Some, however, only accept returns for unopened sheet sets in the original packaging. Others provide longer terms (up to 365 days) with no questions asked, effectively like a free in-home trial.

There are a variety of certifications out there to ensure that consumers are getting high-quality bedding and textiles. One of the most common labels you’ll find on sheets is the OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification, which means that the product has been tested for more than 1,000 harmful substances. Some sheets may also have sustainability labels, like FSC certification, or an Asthma & Allergy Friendly certification from the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America. Keep in mind that more certifications tend to lead to a higher price tag, though—and not all are necessary.

Our favorite cooling sheets range in price from $37 to $322 for a queen-size set. There’s no need to spend hundreds on a set of sheets—you can easily find high-quality cooling sheets for $100-plus. However, certain fabrics like linen will cost more and in return should survive many years of use.

Women’s Health first wrote this story in 2019 and has been continuously testing new cooling sheets as they’re released. During that time, some clear favorites have emerged. For this update, we had several WH staffers and contributors test these products in their own beds. Each sheet set was tested for two to three weeks or longer, and evaluated on their cooling abilities, softness, and durability, among other factors. Testers ranged from those who regularly wake up sweaty to people who consider themselves “neutral” in terms of sleep temperature.

Yes, cooling sheets actually work. They’re designed to be lightweight, breathable, and moisture-wicking, all of which can make you feel cooler when you sleep at night. However, there are a lot of factors that influence how hot you feel at night, including the type of mattress and comforter you have. Ultimately, cooling sheets are one more way to help you feel comfortable, but they shouldn’t be the only thing you use if you tend to run hot while you sleep.

Cotton is usually considered best, but you have a few options to choose from when it comes to cooling materials for sheets.

Bamboo sheets can be cooler than cotton sheets, but that’s not always the case. The weave of your sheets matters. A cotton percale weave sheet can be very cooling and even more cooling than standard bamboo sheets. But cotton is also used to make flannel sheets—which are heat-insulating, not cooling—making it hard to rely on fabric alone when choosing the best cooling sheets.

Thread count is usually linked to the softness of sheets, but it can impact how cool sheets feel. A higher thread count typically means that sheets are denser, which can work against your efforts to stay cool. That’s why Young suggests choosing sheets with a lower thread count, like 400, over much higher thread count options.

Cooling sheets should be washed as often as “regular” sheets, which means they should be washed every week, says Kelly Murray, a certified pediatric and adult sleep coach in Chicago. This will allow you to wash away any allergens, keeping your sheets feeling crisp and fresh, she adds.

By the way, you should wash your cooling sheets before using them, too. "You're washing off any dust the sheets may have collected in the warehouse, which can irritate your respiratory system and lead to sleep issues,” Murray says.

Some cooling sheets, especially those made with natural fibers like cotton and linen, soften with each successive wash. If your new set feels a little too stiff or "crunchy," try running them through a machine wash cycle or two to soften them.

There is an almost universal rule among experts that you should be changing your sheets every week, and Murray concurs. If you don't want to wash your sheets that often, you should consider purchasing an extra set to swap out each week.

As for when it's time to swap out cooling sheets for brand new ones, that's up to you. Murray says she purchases a new set whenever she sees them on sale, but recommends replacing yours about every two to three years.

ICYDK, your body temperature needs to drop about 2 degrees lower at night in order to synthesize melatonin, Murray says. So, it is super important that you create an environment that allows for this. That means ensuring your bedroom is "dark, cool, and quiet" when you're ready for bed.

Other than investing in some cooling sheets, you can also improve your sleep quality by keeping a consistent sleep routine that involves ending screen time at least an hour before you go to bed. "Your body and brain are always looking for patterns throughout the day to know what happens next," Murray says. "So if you have a consistent bedtime routine that's very relaxing, that will trigger the production of melatonin and help your brain to unwind."

#4992. Elon Musk’s SpaceX Gets FCC Approval to Launch AI Data Centers in Space

Elon Musk’s SpaceX Gets FCC Approval to Launch AI Data Centers in Space

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Wednesday authorized SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites designed to operate as data centers in space, giving Elon Musk the regulatory green light to pursue one of his most ambitious artificial intelligence projects yet.

The constellation, called Starmind, will consist of solar-powered computing modules designed to process large amounts of data in orbit for use back on Earth. It marks the first time the U.S. regulator has authorized a satellite constellation specifically designed for this purpose.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short SpaceX with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

“The Starmind & competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America’s lead in Super Intelligence,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr wrote on X.

“Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk replied.

Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world.

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 25, 2026

The FCC even brought a bit of science fiction into its announcement, suggesting the project could bring humanity closer to becoming a Kardashev Type II civilization—a hypothetical society capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its star.

SpaceX originally submitted its proposal in January, with the FCC opening a review in February, shortly after Musk folded his AI startup xAI, the developer of Grok, into SpaceX.

Unlike Starlink satellites, which primarily provide internet connectivity, Starmind satellites would perform computations themselves, exchanging information through laser communications. The authorization also allows SpaceX to use radio frequencies as a backup for communications and emergency satellite controls.

Electricity has become one of the biggest bottlenecks in the AI industry. Companies can spend billions of dollars building data centers and buying chips, only to find that local power grids cannot supply enough electricity to run them.

Satellites operating in certain orbits can receive sunlight almost continuously, making solar panels up to eight times more productive than their counterparts on Earth, according to Google research.

Google is pursuing a similar initiative called Project Suncatcher. The company launched its first prototype in October and selected Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ space company, for another mission scheduled for 2029.

Keeping computers cool in space, despite its reputation for being extremely cold, is surprisingly difficult. The vacuum prevents heat from dissipating through air, meaning satellites need radiators to expel the heat generated by AI chips, which must also withstand exposure to cosmic radiation.

There are environmental concerns, too. The Center for Space Environmentalism warned in September that manufacturing, deploying and eventually deorbiting a constellation of this size could contribute significantly to atmospheric pollution. The FCC said Starmind complies with its orbital debris regulations.

Getting permission to launch a million satellites and actually putting them in orbit are two very different things. During an investment conference earlier this month, Musk estimated that the first Starmind computers could launch in the third quarter of 2027.

SpaceX’s securities disclosures have previously warned investors that its orbital computing business has yet to demonstrate commercial viability and could ultimately prove unsuccessful.

#4989. ‘The time to prepare for a cryptographic breakthrough is before it happens’: Zcash team urges faster deprecation of legacy shielded pool

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

About 400,000 ZEC remains in the Sapling pool, worth about $291 million at current prices.

Zcash Zcash (ZEC) infrastructure team Zakura urged the network to accelerate the deprecation of its legacy Sapling shielded pool, citing speculation of mathematical breakthroughs at AI labs.

In a post early Thursday, Zakura recommended users migrate any ZEC still in Sapling to Ironwood. These shielded pools allow users to hold and transfer ZEC without publicly revealing transaction amounts or sender and recipient addresses.

"The time to prepare for a cryptographic breakthrough is before it happens," the team wrote.

While practical breaking of the pairing-based cryptography used by Sapling remains highly speculative, Zakura also recommended a network upgrade to disable payments into Sapling. Roughly 400,000 ZEC, or approximately 2% of supply, remains in the pool, according to Zakura, worth roughly $291 million at current prices. Zakura said most wallets support both Sapling and Ironwood, and the impact should be minimal, with miners accounting for much of the activity left in Sapling.

"Less than 2.6% of all transactions in the last 30 days use Sapling, and of those, 66% are known miner flows, and it's highly likely most of the remainder are miners as well," the team said.

An earlier Zcash forum proposal in April had suggested waiting a year after a community decision to make Sapling withdrawal-only. At the time, the proposal put its balance at 600,000 ZEC, down from 1.1 million at the start of 2024. Zakura did not suggest a new deadline in its Thursday post.

Zakura pointed to a reported proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and unsubstantiated rumors that AI labs had also made advances in integer factorization, the process of splitting large numbers into their prime factors. The difficulty of that task underpins RSA encryption, which is rarely used in cryptocurrencies, according to the team. Zakura said some math can be used for attacks on both RSA and pairing-based cryptography, so advances in one could help with the other, but the reported Riemann proof and the rumors do not show that either can be broken in practice.

"Practical pairing breaks are highly speculative," Zakura said, adding that transparent transactions and Ironwood do not rely on factoring or pairings.

Nevertheless, a hypothetical break in Sapling's pairing-based proof system would allow forged proofs, Zakura said, putting the funds in the pool at risk. The same cryptography does not secure users' private keys or their cryptographic records of shielded funds, so the team said developers could replace the proof system without replacing those records. However, Zcash would have to freeze Sapling before an attack compromises its state and users could then later recover their funds using a new ECDLP-based or hash-based SNARK, Zakura said.

Separately, the Ethereum Foundation doubled its protocol security team, The Block previously reported, arguing that AI is a "more urgent risk" than quantum computing and recommending Keccak-256 over four competing candidates for Ethereum's planned shift to hash-based cryptography. Zakura said it is also working on a proposal to add hash-based, post-quantum signatures for Zcash transparent transactions using SPHINCS+ with 192-bit security.

#4988. Spain Lets Anti-Money Laundering Unit Freeze Crypto Accounts Without a Judge

Spain has given its financial intelligence unit the power to freeze crypto accounts on its own authority, without first getting a judge’s approval, when it suspects money laundering or terrorist financing.

The change was published in Spain’s official state gazette on Wednesday as part of Royal Decree-Law 44/2026, a sweeping decree that mostly deals with consumer credit contracts and the sale of bad loan portfolios. Its sixth final provision adds a new Article 46 bis to the country’s 2010 anti-money laundering law.

The new article lets the Executive Service of the Commission for the Prevention of Money Laundering and Monetary Offenses, known as Sepblac, suspend or refuse to authorize a transaction in progress. It can also suspend the use of a bank, payment or crypto-asset account, or a business relationship, when there are “indications” that it could be tied to money laundering or terrorist financing.

According to the text, the goal is to preserve the funds while Sepblac carries out its analysis and checks whether the suspicion holds up. If it does, the unit passes the information to the competent authorities so they can take further action.

The decree sets two separate time limits. Sepblac can hold a pending transaction for no more than 10 business days, and it can freeze an account or business relationship for no more than five. Either hold must be lifted sooner if it is no longer needed to preserve the funds.

When the suspicion comes from a suspicious activity report filed by a bank or other regulated firm, Sepblac must issue the suspension within three business days of that report. When the case comes from the unit’s own analysis, the decree says it must act “as soon as possible.”

Once those deadlines pass, the freeze ends unless a court ratifies or extends it at the request of the public prosecutor’s office. Appeals against a court’s decision follow Spain’s criminal procedure law.

The decree also shields Sepblac, its staff and the firms that carry out its orders from liability. Firms that ignore a suspension order commit an offense under the anti-money laundering law. Sepblac can also act at the request of Spanish police and security forces, or of financial intelligence units in other EU states and outside the bloc.

Until now, Sepblac could only use this power when a foreign financial intelligence unit asked it to. The government said in the decree’s preamble that the limit is a deficiency the Financial Action Task Force will assess, and that waiting longer could hurt Spain’s international evaluation.

The government also said the speed of financial transactions, especially online, lets possibly criminal funds move before authorities can finish their analysis. The provision transposes Article 24 of an EU directive adopted in May 2024 on the mechanisms member states must set up to fight money laundering.

The rule takes effect Jan. 25, 2027, two months after the decree’s publication. As a royal decree-law, it must also be put to a vote in Spain’s Congress of Deputies within 30 days to be validated or repealed.

The decree does not name individual crypto platforms, and it is not yet clear how exchanges operating in Spain will receive and carry out the orders. Several European governments have been moving the same way. Poland’s parliament voted 240-202 this month to let officials freeze bitcoin and bank funds of people on a national sanctions list before a court reviews the case.

Other moves in Europe have gone the opposite way. France’s Senate rejected amendments that would have forced holders to declare self-custody wallets worth €100,000 or more, while Binance is closing accounts in four EU countries at the end of the year.

Under the decree, crypto-asset accounts fall under the same five-day freeze limit as bank and payment accounts.

#4985. Researchers Just Figured Out a Way to Detect Ovarian Cancer Earlier Than Ever

More than 21,000 women in the U.S. are diagnosed with ovarian cancer each year. While it’s not the most common cancer in women, ovarian cancer is considered the deadliest cancer in women worldwide because it’s often diagnosed at later stages, has a high rate of recurrence, and is difficult to treat. Right now, the five-year survival rate of ovarian cancer is just 52 percent.

As with most cancers, detecting the disease early may increase the odds of survival. Researchers recently discovered a new way to detect earlier stages of the cancer, potentially helping thousands of women. The Nature Medicine study breaks down the mechanisms of a blood-based test that can detect ovarian cancer in its precancerous stages. In theory, this could dramatically impact survival rates in women. The test is still in the research phases, but doctors agree that something like this is needed. Here’s what they want women to know.

Meet the experts: Diana Pearre, MD, gynecologic oncologist at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA; Abdulrahman Sinno, MD, chief of the division of gynecologic oncology with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System

First, some background: Researchers found that women with early-stage high-grade serous ovarian cancer or serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), which is a precursor to ovarian cancer, have higher-than-usual levels of a type of RNA called Tu-stroma circulating in their blood.

Tu-Stroma is linked with cancer’s early attacks that weaken healthy cells to make room for cancer cell growth. Spotting Tu-stroma means that doctors have an early molecular warning signal that could suggest cancer is developing before a tumor is detected.

The study itself was conducted on hundreds of women around the world with and without cancer and found that the test detected STIC in 92.3 percent of women with the condition. It also correctly identified 98.2 percent of healthy women. They also tried the test on a high-risk group and found that about 72 percent of positive results were accurate, while negative results were almost 100 percent accurate.

But this is still an early discovery, and the researchers point out in the study that more robust research is needed.

“We have very few ways of detecting ovarian cancer,” says Diana Pearre, MD, gynecologic oncologist at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, California. “There are no screening tests.” Instead, doctors rely on pelvic ultrasounds and labs to look for tumor markers.

“Unfortunately, we subject women to surgery if and when they have ovarian masses that are suspicious,” Dr. Pearre says. “Having another tool to help us discriminate which tumors are more suspicious would be very helpful in detecting cancers at an early stage.”

Abdulrahman Sinno, MD, chief of the division of gynecologic oncology with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System, agrees. “Eighty percent of high-grade serous carcinoma is diagnosed in advanced stage with no effective screening strategy,” he says.

Previous screening strategies didn’t work because they only spotted cancer at advanced stages, Dr. Sinno says. “Before this, there was no screening test for average-risk women,” he adds.

We’re not at the stage where this can be rolled out to the general public yet. The blood test is still considered experimental and it’s not a clinically validated. Still, doctors say the news is worth following. “This is a promising discovery-stage result, not a test that is ready for prime time,” Dr. Sinno says.

#4984. Nvidia to Pay $290 Million to Settle Long-Running Crypto Mining Revenue Lawsuit

Nvidia to Pay $290 Million to Settle Long-Running Crypto Mining Revenue Lawsuit

Nvidia has agreed to pay $290 million to settle a shareholder lawsuit dating back to 2018, resolving long-running claims that the chipmaker misled investors about how much of its soaring gaming revenue was actually driven by cryptocurrency miners.

According to a court filing Tuesday, the proposed cash settlement would close a case rooted in the 2017-2018 crypto boom, when miners snapped up Nvidia’s GeForce GPUs to mint coins, with the sales booked as gaming revenue.

As Decrypt reported, shareholders alleged Nvidia downplayed its dependence on that volatile mining demand, leaving investors blindsided when the boom collapsed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In November 2018, the company cut its quarterly revenue forecast as mining demand evaporated, and its stock tumbled roughly 28% over the following two trading sessions.

The settlement covers investors who bought Nvidia stock between Aug. 10, 2017, and Nov. 15, 2018. An analysis commissioned by the plaintiffs estimated Nvidia had understated its crypto-related GPU sales by about $1.1 billion over that stretch.

The company has consistently denied wrongdoing, arguing it could not reliably quantify how much of its gaming revenue stemmed from mining, and it is not admitting liability as part of the deal.

The case has taken a winding, years-long path through the courts. A district court dismissed the suit in March 2021 for failure to adequately allege the executives knew they were misleading investors. A federal appeals court then partly revived it in 2023, keeping the claims alive against Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang while dismissing those against two other executives, including Colette Kress, the finance chief who briefly served as interim CEO during Huang’s recent ouster.

The dispute then reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which heard arguments before dismissing the appeal in December 2024 without ruling on the merits. The district court certified the class in March 2026, and the $290 million figure emerged from mediation led by former federal judge Layn Phillips, whose recommendation both sides accepted in September.

The sum is modest for a company whose market value has swelled into the trillions on the AI boom.

Plaintiffs’ damages expert pegged the maximum the class could have won at trial at about $2.06 billion, meaning the settlement represents roughly 14% of those potential damages, a figure the plaintiffs’ lawyers note compares favorably with typical securities-case recoveries.

Those attorneys said they plan to seek up to 21.4% of the fund, or about $62 million, in legal fees, which they stressed sits below the Ninth Circuit’s 25% benchmark.

The settlement still requires court approval. Under the plaintiffs’ proposed schedule, the court would first decide whether to grant preliminary approval and send notice to affected shareholders, with a final settlement hearing to follow about 130 days later.

Notably, the deal is unrelated to the separate, far more recent turmoil around Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang, whose brief ouster and reinstatement this month over a spy-tinged scandal rattled markets.

For Nvidia, the agreement finally draws a line under one of the last major legal hangovers from crypto’s last great mining frenzy.

#4982. New York Wins $1.37 Billion Judgment Against NovaTech Crypto Ponzi Founders

A New York judge has ordered the founders of NovaTech, a cryptocurrency investment scheme that targeted Haitian communities, to pay more than $1.37 billion, closing out the state’s case against a couple who fled the country rather than answer it.

Justice Anar Rathod Patel of the New York County Supreme Court signed the order on Nov. 24. It holds Cynthia and Eddy Petion and their companies NovaTech Ltd, NovaTech Advisors and NovaPay jointly liable for $1,367,023,585 in disgorgement and interest.

New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the win on Wednesday.

“Today’s historic judgment finally delivers some semblance of justice for the thousands of New Yorkers who were targeted by this merciless scam,” James said. “NovaTech cruelly targeted immigrant families through faith and community groups with the promise of a better life while robbing them of their life savings.”

The award matches what the attorney general’s office asked for in October. The figure starts with the cryptocurrency investors sent to NovaTech’s wallet at payment processor CoinPayments, which totaled about $1.16 billion from August 2019 through May 2023, according to an affirmation filed by the state.

Prosecutors subtracted the roughly $26 million NovaTech actually moved to its trading platform, leaving $1.13 billion in principal. Nine percent annual interest from June 2023 through September 2025 added another $232.5 million.

NovaTech’s traders lost about $18.2 million of the money they did trade, the filing said. Everything else paid out of the wallet, including so-called returns and recruitment bonuses, came from other investors’ deposits.

Cynthia Petion was the only authorized user on the CoinPayments account, and the state says she approved at least $134.5 million in crypto withdrawals to wallets belonging to her and her husband.

The judge also ordered the Petions’ earlier venture, AWS Mining, to pay about $1.46 million. Cynthia Petion owes a separate $4.69 million tied to her promotion of that scheme.

AWS Mining sold crypto mining contracts and promised 15% to 20% monthly returns before it collapsed in 2019, according to the attorney general’s office. The Petions then launched NovaTech, falsely marketed it as a registered hedge fund broker and advertised trading profits of about 2% to 4% a week.

Promoters recruited through prayer groups, WhatsApp chats and ads in Haitian Creole. More than 11,000 New Yorkers invested, alongside what the state called hundreds of thousands of investors worldwide.

NovaTech collapsed in May 2023, and tens of thousands of investors couldn’t withdraw their crypto. The state sued in June 2024.

The Petions never answered the complaint. The court entered a default judgment in August 2025 that found they violated New York’s Martin Act and banned them from the securities, commodities and cryptocurrency industries. They also never produced the investor accounting the court ordered.

Because the money award also came by default, NovaTech’s founders never contested the figures. The order lets the state docket it as a money judgment and begin collection, though it’s unclear how much can be recovered from defendants who left the U.S.

Four of NovaTech’s top promoters settled in October. Martin Zizi, Frantz Ciceron, Ricardo Roy Sr. and James Corbett agreed to pay nearly $6 million combined for the benefit of victims and accepted permanent industry bans.

The judgment lands as regulators step up crypto fraud cases. Last week, the SEC froze assets in a separate $560 million crypto trading Ponzi scheme run out of Indianapolis, weeks after it charged companies in a $130 million crypto case.

“My office will always fight to bring fraudsters who take advantage of hardworking New Yorkers to justice,” James said.

#4978. What Is Artex? The AI Hacking Tool Linked to the US Spy Agency Breach

What Is Artex? The AI Hacking Tool Linked to the US Spy Agency Breach

The AI tool reportedly used to breach a system shared by three U.S. intelligence agencies is already part of the arsenal of at least six hacking groups tracked by Microsoft, according to research published Wednesday.

Artex, a framework originally developed to help cybersecurity professionals find security flaws, was reportedly involved in an intrusion affecting the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

The compromised system analyzes information collected from publicly available sources, according to the Associated Press. The identity of the hackers and the AI model they used remain unconfirmed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In one analysis, Microsoft's threat intelligence team identified both financially motivated criminals and state-sponsored groups using the software, including Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Storm-0940, and Storm-3358. Microsoft did not attribute the spy agency breach to any of them.

“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.

The CIA intrusion, disclosed Tuesday, affected a shared intelligence analysis system that draws on sources such as social media, commercial satellite imagery, and data brokers. A source told Nextgov/FCW that the breach had been resolved and classified systems were unaffected. What information, if any, was stolen remains unclear, though such an intrusion could expose analysts' investigative priorities.

The NSA suffered a similar breach exposing unclassified information, according to the New York Times. Prior, the NSA's classified internal communications network was restored on November 20 after several days of disruption. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton attributed the outage to software patching rather than a cyberattack. The Donald Trump administration has denied that the recent outages were part of a coordinated attack.

Separately, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, a database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide that contains criminal histories, records of missing persons, fugitives, and stolen property. Investigators have not publicly established the extent of the intrusion or whether records were stolen.

Artex is not an AI model like ChatGPT's GPT or Anthropic's Claude. It is an agentic harness, a piece of software that lets language models interact with other programs and perform tasks rather than simply generate text.

A developer known as Autumn-27 published the project on GitHub in July. Written in Go, it was designed for penetration testing, the practice of attempting to break into computer systems with the owner's permission to identify security weaknesses.

The framework divides work among specialized AI agents responsible for planning, carrying out assessments, and reporting their results, according to Google's threat intelligence team. A shared record of findings helps the agents retain context and coordinate their work over lengthy assignments.

The underlying AI is interchangeable. Microsoft says Artex can use commercial and open-weight models, which means the framework is not necessarily subject to the safety policies of any one AI company.

Microsoft says that under certain conditions Artex can obtain lasting access with elevated permissions in minutes, rather than requiring someone to oversee each stage of an operation.

Artex attracted international attention in October after attacks on South Korean financial institutions. A November 13 FBI advisory linked the campaign to the theft of personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people.

Autumn-27 removed the original repository in October following reports of criminal abuse. By early November, researchers had counted more than 1,600 publicly exposed Artex installations, according to the FBI, though that does not mean all were operated by criminals.

Removing an open-source repository does not erase the copies others have downloaded or the independent versions they have created. Microsoft says that this month Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of Artex and began selling access to a commercial offering called Artex Pro.

The problem is not unique to Artex. Security researchers have long released tools that criminals later repurposed, but AI reduces the amount of manual work involved in running them.

The FBI has tracked Artex-related activity across 10 industries since August, including government, defense, finance, and technology.

On November 13, Amazon researchers described campaigns believed to involve Artex, including attempts to steal AI service credentials and circumvent identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

The identity verification system rejected every synthetic video attempt documented by the agents. Amazon also cautioned that it could not independently verify all the outcomes the agents claimed to have achieved.

As Decrypt reported last year, Anthropic said suspected Chinese state-sponsored hackers had already used Claude to automate 80% to 90% of the tactical work in a cyberespionage campaign targeting roughly 30 organizations.

Smaller criminal groups now have access to software that handles some of the coordination previously left to experienced hackers. They still need vulnerable targets, and defenders can still stop them.

Britain's National Cyber Security Centre said Tuesday that it had seen a sharp increase in AI-assisted attacks since September, with criminals exploiting familiar problems such as poorly secured accounts and misconfigured software.

For organizations defending themselves, the immediate priority remains fixing those weaknesses, reducing the number of publicly exposed systems, and improving detection. Britain's cybersecurity agency says today's agentic frameworks are relatively noisy, giving defenders a chance to spot them, though future versions may be harder to detect.

#4973. Russia’s VTB Opens Bitcoin Trading as Central Bank Finalizes Crypto Test

Russian bank VTB began letting brokerage clients buy and sell bitcoin in its investing app on Friday, a day after the Bank of Russia approved the knowledge test every Russian crypto buyer now has to pass.

Starting Nov. 27, clients of VTB’s brokerage can trade cryptocurrencies in the VTB My Investments app, the broker said. For now, the trades happen over the counter rather than on an exchange, and access is limited to qualified investors, the legal term for Russians who meet wealth or experience thresholds, who also pass the new test.

“In our model, access to cryptocurrencies will require qualified investor status and passing special testing,” Andrei Yatskov, head of brokerage services at VTB, said. He said the test would appear in the app on Nov. 27 and work like the bank’s existing tests for other instruments.

VTB handles the buying, storage and record-keeping itself on Russian infrastructure. To trade, clients need to open a separate digital account at VTB’s digital depository, where the crypto is held, on top of their regular brokerage account. The bank received its digital depository and crypto exchange licenses on Oct. 6.

“At the start, we will focus on buying and selling cryptocurrencies, and then we will introduce additional services as regulation develops,” Yatskov said.

The launch came quickly after the regulator moved. On Nov. 26, the Bank of Russia approved the first basic standards for brokers and crypto exchange offices, setting the rules for the test. Every investor has to take it, qualified or not, and it is free.

Buyers must answer at least seven of eight questions correctly. The standard lays out eight topic blocks, from regulation, technical basics and information security to stablecoins, low-liquidity coins, address labeling and blocked transactions, and volatility, with one question drawn at random from each.

Investors who fail can try once more the same day, with different questions. Brokers are barred from sharing the correct answers with clients or telling them which questions they missed. A passing result stays valid for one year from the test date or the latest trade, whichever comes later.

The test was the missing piece for Russian banks. When retail buying became legal on Nov. 17, T-Bank said it was waiting on a market standard for testing, and VTB said it was waiting on the remaining rules. Under the broker standard, the industry’s self-regulatory organization has three working days after publication to send brokers the answer options and correct answers.

Ordinary investors still face tight limits once they pass. Non-qualified buyers can only purchase bitcoin, ether and Tether’s USDT, and no more than 300,000 rubles a year through a single intermediary.

Exchange trading is next. SPB Exchange said Friday it will open spot trading in bitcoin, ether and USDT against the ruble on Dec. 1, after the Bank of Russia added it to the registry of digital depositories on Nov. 27. Trading will run from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Moscow time, with same-day settlement in rubles.

Investors won’t all get in on day one. SPB Exchange said brokers will first use the market to set up their systems, and access will open as each broker is ready. TRX and USDC are also approved, but only for qualified investors, with a start date still to come.

Russian exchanges have been allowed to run organized crypto trading since Nov. 22, once the central bank signs off on their rules. Moscow Exchange has also been aiming to open bitcoin trading on Dec. 1.

“We expect that in 2027, as brokers become ready, investor access to the spot market will expand and new products and investment services will appear,” said Evgeny Serdyukov, SPB Exchange’s chief executive.

#4972. Scheduling Your Day Like This May Reduce Physical Pain and Lessen Depression

Here’s why your body and brain love this.

It can be hard to think of anything else when you’re dealing with physical pain and depression. Though treatments for each are very different, new research suggests that a simple lifestyle trick might help ease symptoms of each: Keeping a consistent schedule.

A recent study published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine makes a solid case for having a routine and dealing with less physical and mental pain. Researchers specifically found that older adults who follow a regular daily schedule tend to have less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they have insomnia.

The findings shouldn’t be interpreted to mean putting yourself on a schedule will magically make your pain and depression disappear. Instead, it suggests that having a daily routine could be a complement to the treatments you’re already doing, like physical therapy, talk therapy, and taking an antidepressant. Here’s what doctors recommend keeping in mind—and why they’re on board with the idea of creating and sticking with a regular schedule.

Meet the experts: Eunjin L. Tracy, PhD, lead study author and director of the Sleep, Health, and Relationships Lab at the University of Missouri; Christopher Winter, MD, a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and the author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It; and Beth Malow, MD, a neurologist and chief of the Division of Sleep Disorders at Vanderbilt Health.

For the study, researchers surveyed 67 older adults—37 of those had insomnia and 30 said they slept well. People who said they experienced insomnia were also likely to report that they had more physical pain and higher levels of depression than those who didn’t have insomnia.

But when the researchers dug deeper, they also discovered that participants who stuck with consistent daily schedules reported less pain and fewer symptoms of depression, whether they struggled with insomnia or not.

“The results suggest that greater behavioral-social rhythm regularity is associated with more favorable health outcomes,” the researchers wrote in the study.

The study simply found an association, so it didn’t prove that sticking with a consistent schedule leads to less pain and depression. But experts say there’s likely something here.

“Regular daily routines help keep the body's internal clock synchronized, and that clock influences many systems tied to mood, pain sensitivity, and metabolism,” says Eunjin L. Tracy, PhD, lead study author and director of the Sleep, Health, and Relationships Lab at the University of Missouri.

A consistent schedule can also help support your nervous system, according to Beth Malow, MD, a neurologist and chief of the Division of Sleep Disorders at Vanderbilt Health. “There are many chemicals that are released into our nervous systems during the day and night,” she says. “When we have a consistent schedule, our brains and bodies are more responsive to these chemicals—think of it similarly to taking a prescription medication at the same time every day.” That can lead to less physical pain and a better mood, Dr. Malow says.

An inconsistent schedule can also interfere with activities that tend to combat depression and pain, like exercise, says Christopher Winter, MD, a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and the author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It.

“It's also possible that other factors, such as personality traits like conscientiousness, contribute both to more regular routines and to better health,” Dr. Tracy says.

Ultimately, doctors say more research is needed. “This is a [well] known relationship, although the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood,” Dr. Winter says.

A schedule only works if it’s one you’ll actually follow. Dr. Winter recommends starting with a consistent wake time. “This tends to lend itself to a routine at least with breakfast and coffee, and helps with bedtime,” he says. Try to be consistent with that bedtime, too, adds Dr. Malow. “Even meals can affect our schedule,” she says. “Try to eat at similar times of the day to promote consistency.”

Dr. Winter calls exercise “a daily requirement,” adding that it should be outside if possible to get exposure to sunlight. And, if you can schedule this at a consistent time in your day, even better.

“You don't need to change everything at once,” Dr. Tracy says. “Start with one anchor, keep it consistent, and build from there.”

#4970. Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

For the second time in weeks, a major Bitcoin mining firm has warned that attackers are siphoning mining rewards by hijacking the internet connections between miners and their pools, a sign that a long-dormant weakness in mining’s plumbing is now being exploited at scale.

Mining software firm Braiins said Wednesday that an attacker struck more than a thousand mining sites in a single second on Nov. 20, rerouting their connections to an impostor pool.

It follows a similar incident just last week, when mining-services firm Luxor reported that hackers had redirected miner rewards, which it tied to AI-assisted attacks.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The two firms described somewhat different mechanisms, but the effect was the same: hashrate quietly diverted away from the miners who produced it.

In its security alert, Braiins stressed the attacker didn’t need to break into any miner or into Braiins Pool itself. Instead, they exploited a long-standing flaw in Stratum V1, the unencrypted, plain-text protocol that carries work between miners and pools and offers no way to verify that the server on the other end is the real pool.

By rerouting traffic, the attacker impersonated the pool, fed miners legitimate-looking jobs, and pocketed the resulting shares under their own account at a separate pool.

The scheme hinged on manipulating the Border Gateway Protocol, or BGP, the trust-based system that tells networks where to route internet traffic. The attacker announced a narrower, more specific block of addresses that included a pool’s Stratum endpoint, causing networks that failed to validate the route to funnel miners’ connections to the impostor.

Hijacked machines kept hashing at full power while their pool dashboards showed zero hashrate, making the theft nearly invisible on-site.

Braiins traced episodes starting in early November across Latin America, mostly Brazil and Argentina, before a larger Nov. 20 wave hit mostly European miners, diverting between 0.6 and 1.9 exahashes per second at a time. The firm characterized the short, escalating bursts as the attacker “testing the waters,” noting the diverted hashrate grew more than tenfold in two weeks.

The technique isn’t new. Braiins noted that Dell SecureWorks documented the same routing trick stealing roughly $83,000 in mining rewards back in 2014, and the firm has warned about “hashrate hijacking” since 2020 as a reason to adopt the encrypted Stratum V2 protocol.

For years, the industry treated it as rare enough to tolerate; now, two firms in a matter of weeks have flagged it hitting miners in the wild.

Braiins urged the whole industry to act, recommending miners move to Stratum V2 or Stratum V1 over TLS with certificate verification, strip out plain-text backup connections, and push network operators to validate routes. It also released a free proxy tool for miners that can’t upgrade.

Any miner still on plain Stratum V1, the firm said, “is a target, on any pool.”

The decision comes after the group met in May in Uzbekistan and identified cross-border digital payments as a new area of cooperation.

China, Japan, South Korea, and ASEAN member countries have agreed to set up a dedicated working group on cross-border digital payments and digital asset regulation.

According to a statement released Thursday, finance and central bank deputies gathered in Kyoto, Japan, this week to review progress in implementing the guidance set earlier by the ASEAN+3 finance ministers and central bank governors.

One major focus of the meeting was technological innovation, with discussions centering around cross-border payments and regulatory approaches to crypto assets. The deputies agreed to form the AMRO Cross-Border Digital Payments Program and a dedicated working group to support further policy talks.

The Kyoto decision is a result of a May meeting in Uzbekistan that identified cross-border digital payments as a new area of cooperation.

At that meeting, the group instructed deputies to establish modalities by the end of 2026 to deepen policy discussions on retail and wholesale payment connectivity, as well as regulatory approaches to stablecoins.

"Building on local currency‑based payment systems, technological innovation in cross‑border payments, such as tokenization, should be pursued in consistency with ongoing global discussions on policy […]," the group said in a May statement.

According to AMRO’s job post published last week seeking a consultant on cross-border retail payments, the initiative could cover research into a range of use cases, including person-to-person and person-to-merchant payments, tourism, e-commerce, and remittances.

Finance ministers and central bank governors are expected to further discuss the matter at the next meeting in Nagoya, Japan, in May 2027.

ASEAN+3 is an international cooperation framework that brings together 11 ASEAN member states and China, Japan, and South Korea. The 14 economies regularly convene to discuss political-security, economic, and socio-cultural matters.

The push for closer regional cooperation comes as Asian economies step up efforts to explore and test stablecoin and tokenization initiatives. Last month, the central banks of Malaysia and Thailand joined Singapore's BLOOM initiative to work on cross-border payments involving stablecoins and tokenized deposits.

Japan's top financial regulators are also studying tokenization of Japanese government bonds and a blockchain-based settlement system for stocks and Japanese government bonds. South Korea, meanwhile, is preparing tokenized securities from 2027 and local won stablecoins under its draft Digital Asset Basic Act.

Earlier this month, the central banks of the UK, Singapore, and Thailand also said they completed foreign exchange settlement trial linking traditional and tokenized systems.

#4967. Binance Fully Lifts Withdrawal Suspension a Month After $6.3 Billion Hack

Binance has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it put in place after last month’s record $6.3 billion hack, saying its recovery work is complete and that withdrawals are open across nearly all networks.

“Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted,” the exchange said in an X post Thursday afternoon. A small number of networks remain paused for maintenance, which Binance called standard practice and said was unrelated to the hack.

The update closes out a month of phased reopenings. Binance confirmed the breach on Oct. 29, saying its initial investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that gave the attacker access to a service container, which was then used to submit unauthorized withdrawals.

The world’s largest crypto exchange stopped all customer withdrawals for two days after the theft, Reuters reported. When they first reopened, customers pulled a net $4.7 billion off the platform, Binance said on Nov. 2.

Binance said on Nov. 12 that it had completed coverage of the affected assets with more than $6.34 billion of company funds. The money came from a partial draw on its Secure Asset Fund for Users, part of its futures insurance fund and its corporate treasury, and the exchange pledged to rebuild SAFU to about $1 billion.

Coverage is not the same as recovery. Binance replaced the stolen tokens from its own books, while about $2.85 billion of the stolen funds have been frozen remotely by the companies that issue them. The rest remains in the hands of the attackers.

U.S. authorities have blamed North Korean hackers for the theft, which North Korea denies. On Nov. 23, the Justice Department moved to forfeit more than $1.1 billion in USDC that Circle froze, and said the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion since the attack.

The unfrozen funds are on the move. North Korean launderers have stepped up transfers through THORChain and a coinjoin service in recent days, blockchain researchers told Reuters, as part of an operation spanning tens of thousands of transactions across blockchains.

Chainalysis and Elliptic estimate that more than $600 million of the stolen crypto has passed through THORChain, though Elliptic said that figure could count funds that went through more than once. TRM Labs estimates THORChain earned as much as $1 million in fees from the swaps.

Separately, $342 million has moved through a coinjoin service mostly coordinated by a pseudonymous figure named Kruw, Elliptic said. A coinjoin combines coins from many users into a single transaction, so their origin is no longer visible on the blockchain. Elliptic has said the launderers will still need other services, such as over-the-counter brokers, to turn the coins into cash.

The FBI on Oct. 31 published wallet addresses used by the attacker and asked crypto service providers, including the network of computers that runs THORChain, to block them. In a video posted Thursday, THORChain co-founder Chad Barraford said 98% of trading on the network was for people’s “own individual financial freedom and liberty.”

THORChain, which describes itself as decentralized, says on its website that it does not “censor” transactions or run Know-Your-Customer checks. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, called the FBI’s move to single out the network’s operators “pretty extraordinary.”

Redbord said the laundering could take months or even years, and that cashing out even a fraction would be a windfall for North Korea. The total stolen from Binance equals about a sixth of the country’s estimated gross domestic product.

“They don’t have to get a lot off in order to make this all worthwhile for them,” Redbord said.
